en: The Lineage of the Elements (Dhātuvaṃsa) Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
1. The Account of the Tathāgata’s Arrival.
Having paid homage to the peerless Fully Enlightened One, the pure Dhamma, and the unsurpassed Saṅgha,
I shall proclaim this exposition of the lineage of the relics.
Three times did the Protector come to the delightful island of Laṅkā.
"Desiring the welfare of beings and the long endurance of the Dispensation,
the Protector went there three times"— thus, having turned [the wheel] throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*),

the Blessed One, who has become a protector and refuge by means of producing mundane and supramundane happiness for those who have reached a state of being without refuge, [taught] the path consisting of the Three Jewels of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.
While explaining [the matter], he went to the island of Laṅkā three times. Regarding his first journey there:

having ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and sat down facing the east, even before the sun had set, he scattered the host of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he recollected his former births;
in the middle watch, he attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; and at the conclusion of the final watch—
Having applied his knowledge to the mode of conditions and penetrated the omniscient wisdom adorned with the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and other qualities,
he spent seven weeks in succession at the site of the Bodhi-maṇḍa; then, on the eighth week,
while seated at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he fell into a state of inactivity through reflecting upon the profundity of the Dhamma.
Having been entreated by the Great Brahmā Sahampati and his retinue of ten thousand Brahmas to teach the Dhamma, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye;
recollecting the great benefit to be derived from the group of five monks, he rose from his seat, went to the city of Kāsī,
and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, bestowing the Deathless upon eighteen koṭis of Brahmas headed by Aññā Koṇḍañña.
Having set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion on the fifth day of the fortnight, he established all five members of the group of five as Arhats.
On that very same day, he bestowed the fruit of stream-entry upon the noble youth Yasa during the night, and on the following day, he granted him Arhatship.
Furthermore, having led his fifty-four companions to the state of Arhatship, there were thus sixty-one Arhats in the world.
Having spent the rains retreat among those born [into the world] and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, he dispatched the monks in all directions, saying, "Go forth, monks, on your journey.
Traveling himself toward Uruvelā, he converted the thirty youths of the Bhaddavaggiya group in a cottonwood grove along the way;
having ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehi-bhikkhu*), he proceeded to Uruvelā and performed three thousand five hundred miracles.

Bestowing [his teachings] upon Uruvelakassapa and the others, he remained right there while training those three brothers, the matted-hair ascetics, who were accompanied by a retinue of a thousand such ascetics.
Later on, the inhabitants of the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha provided Uruvelakassapa with the materials for a great sacrifice.
Overcome by desire, he thought: "If this Great Ascetic [should come] into the midst of this assembly..."
“I shall perform a miracle; otherwise, my gain and honor will diminish.

Knowing his inclination to proceed thus, [the Bodhisatta] brought almsfood from Uttarakuru early in the morning, partook of that meal at Anotatta, and on the evening of the Phussa full-moon uposatha day, he arrived at Laṅkādvīpa for the sake of the island of Laṅkā.
On the southern bank of the Mahāgaṅgā on that island, in the Mahānāgavana garden— extending three *yojanas* in length and measuring one *yojana* in width—
in the midst of a gathering of *yakkhas*, at the very spot where the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Thūpa was later established,
he stood suspended in mid-air and, manifesting rain, wind, and darkness, struck terror into them. Overwhelmed by fear, they...
“Whose deed is this? they wondered, and looking here and there, they saw the Blessed One sitting in the air.
Having seen him, they begged the Blessed One for safety.
The Blessed One said to them, “If you desire safety, give me space for my seat. They all—

They gave him a place to sit. Having taken a seat and dispelled their fear, the Blessed One spread out his leather mat upon the ground provided by them and sat down. While sitting, the Blessed One stretched out the leather mat.
Those yakkhas, terrified and trembling, unable to go elsewhere, gathered together all around on the shore of the ocean.
They were there. The Teacher, having brought Giridīpa by means of his supernormal power, showed it to them.
When they had been established there, he returned them to their original places and withdrew even the spread-out piece of hide.
At that moment, devas gathered from here and there. In that assembly, he taught the Dhamma, and there was a realization of the Dhamma for many millions of beings.
They became established in the Refuges and the Precepts, and were beyond counting.
However, when the Great Sumanadeva attained the fruit of stream-entry on Mount Sumanakūṭa, he requested from the Blessed One, his object of worship, [a relic].
Being thus entreated by him, the Blessed One touched his head with his hand, took some hair-relics, and gave them to him. Having given them, he [circumambulated] the island of Laṅkā three times.
Having performed a circumambulation, recited the protective Paritta, and established a guard, he returned once more to Uruvelā.
Taking the hair-relics in a golden casket, he erected a stupa adorned with various jewels at the place where the Teacher had sat;
having covered it above with finials made of sapphire, he dwelt there, making offerings of perfumes, garlands, and other honors.

When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the Elder named Sarabhū, a disciple of Sāriputta who was an arahant with taints destroyed, used his supernormal power to take the neck-bone of the Tathāgata from the funeral pyre.

He enshrined it in that Indanīla jewel stupa, and having caused a stupa twelve cubits high to be built of stone resembling clouds, he departed. After him came Cūḷābhaya, the brother of King Devānampiyatissa.
Upon seeing that wonderful cetiya, Prince Nāma became deeply inspired with faith and, covering it, established a cetiya thirty cubits in height.
Later, King Abhaya Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, having covered that as well, had a kañcuka-cetiya (a casing-shrine) eighty cubits high constructed.
Thus should the account of the establishment of the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Thūpa be understood in detail.
Having attained enlightenment at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Bull among Men, sat there for seven days;
thereafter, he performed a miracle.
Then, standing slightly to the northeast, the Victor sat cross-legged.
With an unwinking eye, he gazed upon it for seven days.
Having paced back and forth for seven days upon the jewel-studded walkway,
the Victor, having discerned the sublime Dhamma within that treasure-house, remained there.
For seven days at Ajapāla, he experienced the bliss born of concentration;
and at the delightful Mucalinda tree, he experienced the supreme bliss of liberation.
He dwelt for seven nights and days at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree.
Then Sakka offered water for rinsing the teeth to the Teacher.
The four World-Protectors brought a stone bowl, and the Leader, having arranged them one by one in a set of four, resolved upon it through his supernormal power.
Then the merchants presented him with stirred milk-rice and honey-cakes.
There, having accepted it, the Jina performed his meal.
Both Tapussa and Bhallika took refuge in him;
they went for refuge to that Teacher, having offered him their hair.
Having returned to their own kingdom, the two lay brothers, the upāsakas,
built a beautiful stūpa and paid homage to it and made offerings.
Thus did the Leader spend those seven weeks.
Requested by Brahmā to set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, the Teacher then went to Bārāṇasī and turned the Wheel of Dhamma.
When the Dhamma was taught, Koṇḍañña attained the fruit of stream-entry.
When the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion, eighteen koṭis of Brahmās and incalculable deities attained the fruit of stream-entry.
On the first day of the waxing moon, Vappa attained it; on the second, Bhaddiya.
On the third day Mahānāma, and on the fourth Assaji;
having gathered them all together, these five members of the group of five,
he taught them the *Anattasutta* (Discourse on Non-Self) with the fruit of the summit of enlightenment.
Having attained enlightenment, he [taught] the group of five headed by the Elder Yasa on the fifth day;
thereafter, the thirty princes of the Bhaddavaggiya group along the way.
Then, having gone to Uruvelā, known as Uruvelā—
Having been authorized by Uruvelā,
the Victor tamed the Nāga of Uruvelā; having seen that various Nāgas such as Ura were tamed through his taming power,
they invited the Tathāgata after witnessing that miracle.
"Having dwelt right here in this forest grove,
O Great Sage, we all shall serve you with a regular meal.
When the great sacrifice of Uruvelakassapa has been prepared,"
Knowing his own desire for him to come,
the Supreme among Bipeds took alms from Uttarakuru,
ate at Lake Anotatta, and returned himself at the time of evening.
In the ninth month from his enlightenment,
on the full moon day of Phussa, the Jina arrived at Laṅkādīpa to purify it.
Having subdued the yakkhas and bestowed the relics, the Sambuddha, the Leader, departed.
Having gone to Uruvelā, the Victor dwelt there in the forest.
The account of the first journey is complete.
However, during his second journey, while residing at the Great Monastery of Jetavana in the fifth year after the Enlightenment, [he visited] Cūḷodara and Mahodara.

Seeing that a battle had been set up by his maternal uncle and nephew, the two nāgas, near a jeweled couch, he himself took his bowl and robes and went to Nāgadīpa on the Uposatha day during the dark fortnight of the month of Citta.
Sitting in the air in the midst of their battle, he created darkness. Having reassured them when they were overcome by that darkness, he showed them light.
For the sake of creating harmony among those who had become his refuge, he taught the Dhamma like one shaking a tree laden with fruit.
Both of them, having gained confidence in the Dhamma, gave that very seat to the Tathāgata.
Seated upon the seat and satisfied with divine food and drink, the Blessed One delivered a discourse of thanksgiving and established eighty million *nāgas* in the refuges.
And he established them in the precepts. At that assembly, Mahodara’s maternal uncle, the Naga king named Maṇiakkhika, requested the Blessed One to come again at a favorable time.
The Blessed One, having consented by remaining silent, went to Jetavana itself;
for in this way he would visit Nāgadīpa.
The Conqueror of Māra, the All-Knowing One, the Wise,
endowed with compassion, having tamed the Nāgas,
went to dwell in Jeta’s Grove as the Lord of Sages.
The account of the second journey is complete.
Regarding the third journey, however, while the Blessed One was dwelling at the Great Monastery of Jetavana in the eighth year after his enlightenment, he said:
"After my parinibbāna, the Dispensation will be established on the island of Tambapaṇṇi; that island shall abound with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, and others."
It will be frequented by the noble assembly and illuminated by the glow of the saffron robes.
Among my four canine relics, one canine tooth, the right eye-tooth relic, and the frontal bone relic shall be obtained by the inhabitants of Rāmagāma;
these as a single portion, along with many other bodily relics and hair relics, shall be established right there in many thousands of monasteries.
"And there will be a great multitude of people established in faith in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.
Therefore, it is fitting that you go to the island of Laṅkā, attain meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) there, and then return," he thought, and addressed the Elder Ānanda:
"Ānanda, [go] to the five hundred great Bhikkhus who have attained the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*) and whose taints are destroyed."
He announced: "We must go together. The Elder Ānanda announced this to five hundred bhikkhus dwelling in the city of Kapilavatthu who were great arahants with taints destroyed.
Having been informed, those five hundred arahants, carrying their bowls and robes, paid homage to the Teacher and stood with palms joined in reverence.

Not far from the Teacher’s perfumed chamber named Salalā, there was a pond with beautiful steps, filled with white, yellow, blue, red, and white lotuses, water-born lilies, hundred-petaled and thousand-petaled varieties, and various fragrant flowers such as the *sogandhika*;
its cool, sweet, and delightful water was clear, level to the brim, and pleasant enough for a crow to drink;
it was surrounded by various and variegated trees such as *sāla*, *salala*, *campaka*, *asoka*, and *nāga* trees, all bearing blossoming flowers and fruit.
In that place there was a lotus pond, its banks well-adorned and exceedingly delightful.
Therein dwelt a powerful Nāga king named Sumanā, surrounded by about sixteen thousand Nāga maidens, enjoying great glory and prosperity.
Having beheld the Tathāgata’s physical form, which had reached the pinnacle of beauty, he experienced great happiness and joy.
Experiencing this, he placed his own mother, Nandana, in the position of a teacher and, while performing service for her, continued to dwell in that very lotus pond.
But the Teacher, having made arrangements for his departure, called out to the Naga king Sumana who was standing nearby, saying, "Come along with your retinue. He replied, "Very well."
Having accepted [the request], he took six million nāgas from his own retinue and, making a parasol out of a *supuppita* campaka tree, held it over the Tathāgata to ward off the rays of the sun.
Then the Blessed One, shining like a golden mountain enveloped by the sun’s rays, took his bowl and robe and rose into the sky. Surrounding the Teacher—
Those five hundred who had destroyed the taints also stood there, each taking their own bowl and robe, and having ascended into the air, they surrounded the Teacher.

Surrounded by those five hundred who had destroyed the taints, the Teacher went to Kalyāṇī on the full-moon uposatha day of the month of Visākha and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the center of the magnificent pavilion, surrounded by those five hundred who had destroyed the taints.
Then the Naga king named Maṇiakkhika, having gratified the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with many kinds of divine hard and soft foods, sat down to one side.
The Teacher, after giving him a blessing of thanksgiving for the meal, displayed the imprint of his foot upon a cluster of jasmine flowers;
then, seated at the base of that mountain on a spot of ground strewn with various trees, he spent the day in meditation.
Emerging from there, he entered a meditative attainment at the site of the Dīghavāpi Cetiya. The great earth, bounded by the waters, shook a hundred times and a thousand times.
Having stationed the divine son named Mahāsena there for protection, he emerged from that state and likewise entered a meditative attainment at the site of the Mahāthūpa. The great earth...

In the same way, the great earth shook. There too, having stationed the divine son Visālarūpa to provide protection, he emerged from that state and likewise entered the attainment of cessation at the site of the Thūpārāma Cetiya. The great earth shook in the same way.
And there, having turned back the divine son Pathavipāla for the sake of protection, he emerged from that state.
Having gone to the site of the Maricavaṭṭi Cetiya, he entered meditative absorption together with five hundred bhikkhus.
The earth shook in that very same way. At that spot, he stationed the deva-son Indaka to provide protection.
Then, emerging from that state, he likewise entered absorption at the site of the Kācara Village Cetiya. The earth shook in that very same way.
It trembled. (At that place, he assigned the divine son Mahāghosa to take up guard.

Having stationed the divine son named Mahāghosa at this site of the Great Cetiya to take up guard, he emerged from there and entered meditative absorption in the same manner at the site of the Tissa Mahāvihāra Cetiya. The earth likewise [trembled].

The earth shook. There, having appointed the goddess named Maṇimekhala to guard it, he entered that same meditative attainment at the site of the Nāgamahāvihāra Cetiya; the earth shook in the same way. There too, he stationed the divine son named Mahinda to provide protection.
Then, emerging from that state, [he went] to the place called Seru on the southern bank of the Mahāgaṅgā.
‘At the end of this aeon, a most enchanting shrine, resembling a mass of water-bubbles or froth, will be established upon the tip of the trunk of the boar named Varāha.
Having spoken thus, he entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) together with five hundred arahants whose taints were exhausted.
[The earth] was like the wheel of a potter spinning upon thick, solid ground, or like the rutting ichor flowing from a great lordly elephant.
Like the sound of a machine for crushing sugarcane and like the cry of a partridge, they roared a hundred times and a thousand times;
as if filled with joy, they caused the entire island of Laṅkā to resound and tremble.
Then, emerging from there, they took flowers from a *campaka* tree standing in the hands of King Sumananāga, offered them there, and [repeated] again and again—
He looked at him. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he asked, "Venerable Sir, what should I do?

He said, "Guard this place. Upon hearing this, he replied, "Venerable Sir, while I am guarding your Gandhakuṭī, [I shall behold] its beauty of form, adorned with the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide aura, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man."
To him who was beholding the unsurpassed vision, he— like a young lion roaring a lion’s roar upon a slab of ruby,
like a great rain-cloud thundering, like the celestial Gaṅgā descending from the sky, and like one stringing together a garland of jewels—
emitted a voice worthy of being heard, endowed with the eight factors, uttering a Brahma-like sound through various methods.
As I listen to the sweet preaching of the Dhamma—capable of delivering those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra—who speak with diverse discourse that flows like a stream of nectar;

and as I behold the eighty great disciples, such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who have reached the pinnacle of knowledge and supernormal power—it is here that I find my dwelling pleasing. I am unable to dwell elsewhere apart from you.
The Blessed One, having heard his words, said: "O King of Nagas, this region is a place where you have resided for a long time.
It was at this very spot that the relics of the Blessed One Kakusandha were established. At that time, you yourself were the Naga King named Varanidda;
having taken charge of the protection of those relics, you remained here for a long time, making offerings of perfumes, garlands, and the like."
...dwelt there. Furthermore, the relics of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana were established in this very place;

at that time, you yourself, having become a son of the gods named Jayasena, took charge of the protection of those relics, performed worship with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and dwelt right there for a long time. Furthermore, the relics of the Blessed One Kassapa [were established] in this very place.
It was established. At that time, you yourself were the Naga king named Dīghasāla;
having taken charge of the protection of that relic, you dwelt there performing worship with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
However, after I have attained Parinibbāna, the great King Kākavaṇṇatissa will establish my forehead-relic in this very place. Therefore, you [should protect] this spot.

Having said, "Provide protection," and having established him in the five precepts, he circumambulated the site of the shrine together with the five hundred who had destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
Then, saying, "Be heedful," he rose into the air and returned to Jetavana.
Meanwhile, the mother of that city king, named Indamānavikā, arrived, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and stood to one side.
"Venerable sir, where is my son, the nāga king named Sumana? he asked.
"Your son is in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, near the lake called Seru on the southern bank of the Mahāvālukagaṅgā.
Having entered the Varāha-saṇḍiya-samādhi and taken with him about six million nāgas as his retinue, he has paid homage to the Teacher and said: 'Venerable sir, from here..."
"From this day forward, it will be difficult for you to see me; forgive my transgression," he said, confessing his fault.

Then, taking with him a great wealth of elephants, he went into the presence of his son, Sumananāgarāja, and having enjoyed the great prosperity of sovereignty right there while providing protection, he dwelt for a long time.
Possessing great wisdom, great faith, a great hero, and a great sage,
endowed with great power and adorned with great virtues,
he went to Tambapaṇṇi with a mind full of compassion for sentient beings.
Having gone to the island of Nāgavara, the wise one went to Jetavana.
Possessing supreme wisdom and bestowing the gift of essence,
he was exceedingly delightful, the sole eye of the entire world.
Bearing exceedingly great virtues, he who is capable of leading all beings upon that supreme path,
possessing vast compassion, came to this beautiful island to deliver them.
The account of the third journey is completed.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Departure of the Tathāgata," in the *Dhātuvamsa* composed for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the noble ones.
Having come to Tambapaṇṇi with a mind full of compassion for sentient beings,
he returned once more to Nāgadīpa and went to the excellent Jetavana.
He whose essence is supreme wisdom, who delights in the gift of the essence,
who is most charming through his great fortitude, the sole leader of the entire world,
[taught] the path that is uniquely peaceful and delightful through its many virtues.
"Because of his exceedingly vast compassion, he came to Laṅkā, the beautiful island"—thus it is seen in the *Dhātuvamso* composed in the Sinhalese language. 2.
The Account of the Parinibbāna.
But the Teacher, having taught the Dhamma of the scriptural tradition of the Three Piṭakas for forty-five years thereafter,
and having rescued those susceptible to instruction from the cycle of existence by means of their attainment of the four noble paths and fruits and established them in Nibbāna,
dwelt in his final period near the city of Vesālī, depending upon the Cāpāla Shrine; and at that time, Māra [approached] him for the sake of his Parinibbāna.
Being mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-force. Ānanda alone knew that it had been relinquished;

there was no one else at all who knew. Therefore, thinking, "I shall inform the community of monks as well," he went to the Great Monastery of Jetavana, assembled the entire community of monks, and said: "Monks, before long for the Tathāgata..."
"Within one month my final *parinibbāna* will take place;

you should all be united and act with one accord regarding the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), and do not engage in dispute. Accomplish the three trainings through diligence.
Having said this, on the following day, after walking for alms in Vesālī and returning from his almsround, he went to Bhaṇḍagāma.
From Bhaṇḍagāma he went to Hatthigāma; from Hatthigāma to Ambagāma; from Ambagāma to Jambugāma;
from Jambugāma to Nigrodhagāma; from Nigrodhagāma to Bhoganagara; from Bhoganagara to Pāvānagara;
and from Pāvānagara he arrived at the city of Kusinārā. Standing there between the twin sāla trees, he addressed the Elder Ānanda and lay down on his right side.
"Having prepared a couch, Ānanda, spread it out; I am weary and will lie down," he said.

Hearing this, the Elder Ānanda prepared a couch with its head toward the north, spread a fourfold-layered outer robe over it, and—having not lain down for forty-five years since his attainment of Buddhahood—lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising.
Wandering through existence in the past,
endowed with compassion for infinite beings,
he performed no small amount of meritorious deeds.
The Protector, for the welfare of the world, attained peace. For even he,
though possessing the ten powers,
lay down in the midst of Yama’s halls, his strength exhausted.
Having formed this perception, he who was possessed of psychic power failed to exert himself and thus entered the mouth of Māra.
At that moment, the twin sāla trees burst into full bloom. Not only did the twin sāla trees blossom, but...
Then, indeed, in the ten-thousandfold world system, even the *sāla* trees in the world-systems blossomed.
Not only did the *sāla* trees blossom beautifully, but whatever species of trees were capable of bearing flowers or fruit, all of them took up both flowers and fruit.
Among the waters, there were water-lotuses; on the land, there were land-lotuses; and upon the trunks [of trees], there were trunk-lotuses.
Upon the branches were branch-lotuses; upon the creepers were creeper-lotuses; in the sky hung hanging-lotuses;

and upon the stone slabs on the backs [of the elephants], hundred-petaled lotuses appeared in full bloom. From the earth up to the Brahma-world, the ten-thousandfold world-system became like a single string of garlands.
From the sky, the gods rained down divine mandārava, pāricchattaka, and koviḷāra flowers.
They scattered sandalwood powder, and celestial musical ensembles resounded in the sky.

There were many thousands of wonders. While such extraordinary honors were being performed, having guided the wanderer Subhadda in the first watch of the night, and having instructed the deities of the ten-thousandfold world system in the middle watch, at the conclusion of the final watch—
Having entered the first jhāna and emerged from it, he entered the second jhāna and the fourth jhāna.
Emerging from that, he entered the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Emerging from that, he entered the attainment of cessation. Emerging from that, he entered the first jhāna.
He attained the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna. Emerging from there, he passed away into the element of nibbāna without residue right then and there.
Having destroyed the great darkness of delusion that clings to the hearts of beings—
Shining like the sun, he who was compassionate toward the world,
having performed much benefit for beings for forty-five years,
that Conqueror has now attained final nibbāna like a mass of fire.
But when the Blessed One had thus attained final Nibbāna, Vissakamma, the son of the devas,
fashioned a precious casket the size of the Tathāgata’s body; having wrapped the Tathāgata’s body in pure cotton cloth, he placed it in the precious casket,
filled it with scented oils, covered it with another casket, prepared a funeral pyre of all kinds of fragrant wood, and for the most part...
The deities, having taken vases of red sandalwood and placed them upon the funeral pyre, were unable to set fire to it. Why was this?
Because the Elder Mahākassapa had not yet arrived. That venerable Elder Mahākassapa was, for the most part, dear and pleasing to many devas;
indeed, there is no measure to those who, having given alms to the Elder, were reborn in the heavenly realms.
Therefore, when the deities did not see their own family preceptor among that assembly, they looked about, wondering, "Where is our Elder Mahākassapa?
Upon learning that he had set out on the road together with his retinue of approximately five hundred bhikkhus, they made this resolve:
"As long as the Elder has not arrived here, let the funeral pyre not ignite. In that regard—
At that time, the Elder arrived together with approximately five hundred monks who were for the most part observers of the thirteen ascetic practices;
having circumambulated the funeral pyre three times clockwise, he stood at the side of the feet and said:
"Venerable Sir, from the time of making the formal aspiration at the feet of the Teacher Padumuttara one hundred thousand aeons ago, [this resolve] has never been abandoned."
"He has arrived. Now is my opportunity to see him," he resolved, and grasping [the Buddha's] feet, he prepared to pay homage.
Then the Elder Mahākassapa, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, arranged his robe over one shoulder and extended his joined palms in reverence.
Having performed the circumambulation three times and stood at the edge of the footprint, he made this resolution:
"May the feet of the Victor be established upon my head.
Simultaneously with that resolution, the funeral pyre and the cloths were shattered.
Then his feet emerged like the moon from behind a thick cloud.
Having taken them up with both hands and placed them upon his own head,
he paid homage at the Teacher’s feet, asked for forgiveness, and dismissed him.
Just as the full moon had entered the funeral pyre,
the great multitude, seeing this marvel, raised a cry.
Rising up toward the east, they paid homage as if to the sun setting.
As his feet disappeared, the great multitude wept.
Then the Malla kings, saying, "We shall perform the funeral rites for the Blessed One's body," dressed themselves in various garments and ornaments and surrounded him.
Thereupon, the kings and the people began to prepare the fire. At that time, Sakka [thought]: "But as for me..."
"When the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, Sakka, the King of Devas, will extend the radiance of his jewel and perform the funeral rites for my body with the fire that issues from it.
At the conclusion of the jewel-fire, humans shall provide the fire.

Having thus meditated upon these words of the Buddha, he circumambulated [the body] three times keeping it to his right, performed the funeral rites for the Blessed One's body, and resolved: "Let the fire rise up on all sides!"

At that moment, the fire on the funeral pyre ignited spontaneously. As the Blessed One’s body was being consumed, the relics remained as the only residue, with skin, hide, flesh, sinews, bones, and marrow entirely consumed, appearing like jasmine buds or a heap of pearls.
Even at the time of his final passing, there was universal lamentation;
there was great wailing, as if the very earth were being torn asunder.
Through the power of the deity, the Teacher’s funeral pyre ignited by itself all at once from every side.
Both the cloth that was inside and the cloth that was entirely outside—
Two pieces of cloth did not burn at all between those cloths;
just as there is neither soot nor ash from a lamp whose oil is exhausted,
so too nothing was seen of the Buddha’s body as he meditated.
The relics remained like jasmine buds, resembling washed pearls, and appearing with the luster of gold.
There were four teeth, the cranial protuberance, and two collarbones, all possessing great power.
The remaining elements were not scattered there, but were indeed strewn about.
That element was minute, the size of a mustard seed;
the intermediate elements were in the middle, the size of a broken grain of rice.
The relics were large, the size of split mung beans in the middle;
through the power of the Buddha’s resolve, they became three colors.
The elder Sāriputta had a disciple named Sarabhu.
Taking the collar-bone relic of the Jina from the funeral pyre, he,
together with a thousand disciples, placed it upon the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Cetiya;
having thus established the shrine, the Sage departed for Kusinārā.
The sage, possessing the six super-knowledges, having attained mastery, peaceful and compassionate,
suddenly seized the left canine tooth right from the funeral pyre;
even though it had fallen from the sky or emerged from the sāla tree.
Surging up from all sides, they extinguished the fire with water.
All the hosts of the Malla kings extinguished that funeral pyre of the Lord of the World, the Great Sage, with water scented with every kind of perfume.
Thus, on the Vesākha full-moon Uposatha day, which was a Tuesday, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who excels all in compassion, attained final Nibbāna.
For the sake of gathering together devas and humans, he remained for seven days and nights upon the funeral pyre between the twin Sāla trees.
Thereafter, he remained for another seven days and nights above the height of one hundred cubits until his cremation by fire.
It was for seven days and nights.

Then, for seven days, while the Malla princes of Kusinārā were extinguishing the funeral pyre with scented water, streams of water issued forth from the *sāla* trees and extinguished the pyre. Thereafter, the relics of the One of Ten Powers...
Having placed [the body] in a golden casket, they set it in the assembly hall in their own city, constructed a cage of spears, and had it surrounded by walls of bows;
for seven days, the Malla princes paid honor with dance, song, instrumental music, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Then those Malla kings [prepared] a beautiful place, like the assembly hall of the gods...
Then, having plastered the assembly hall on every side,
and having decorated the road as far as the Makuṭa Cetiya,
he placed the golden casket containing the relics upon the back of an elephant.
Having honored [the relics] even with perfumes and other offerings, they played a most excellent game;
then, having brought them into the city, they placed the Conqueror’s relics upon a couch in a delightful assembly hall on the tenth floor.
Then they had couches placed on all sides of the assembly hall beneath the canopy.
They had elephants stationed there, then horses, then chariots;
then the warriors surrounded one another, and then the archers.
Thus they had it enclosed on all sides for a league by turns;
then they honored him with dances, songs, and instrumental music.
The account of the Parinibbāna is complete.
Then, having heard that the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, King Ajātasattu sent a message to the Mallas of Kusinārā:
"I too am a khattiya, and the Blessed One was a khattiya; I shall erect a stūpa and hold a great festival for the Teacher’s bodily relics.
By that same means, the Licchavi kings in Vesālī and the Sakyans in Kapilavatthu [sent similar messages].

The Bulayas from Allakappa, the Koliyas from Rāmagāma, the Brahmin from Veṭhadīpaka, and the Pāvāvakas from Pāvā, having sent messengers with the message, all gathered together and instigated a dispute with the people of Kusinārā.
Their teacher was a Brahmin named Droṇa. He said to them: "Sirs, do not engage in this quarrel and dispute. For us..."

Having said, "The Blessed One is indeed a teacher of patience," he stated that it was improper to engage in strife over the bodily remains of one so endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.
(And King Ajātasattu and the Licchavi lords of men...)
The Sakyas, the Allakappas, and the Koḷiyas, as well as Rāma and Veṭhadīpa the brahmin,
and the Mallas of Pāvā— the Mallas themselves quarreled with one another for the sake of the relics.
This being so, the brahmin Doṇa then spoke these words:
"May you, sirs, listen to my speech, which is beneficial and conducive to welfare.
At the time of the seer Khantivādī, when Prince Dhammapāla was a child..."
When Bhuridatta, Campeyya, and Saṅkhapālaka were being sacrificed,
our Leader of the World, the Victor, did not give way to anger during the time of the Mahākapi Jātaka, but instead showed only patience toward others.
Regarding what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, pleasure and pain, gain and loss,
fame and disrepute— the one who is such, endowed with the marks of perfection,
what need is there to speak of his patience? Thus, in your dispute, this conflict is not good.
"May you all be united, harmonious, and joyful.
Let us divide the relics of the Tathāgata into eight portions,
so that stupas may be erected everywhere and many people may find faith."
"In that case, O Brahmin, divide it into eight portions;
let the stūpas be expanded, for many people have placed their faith.
When this was said, the Brahmin Doṇa, the senior of the assembly, [acted accordingly].
Having fashioned the gold into a *nāḷi* measure, he divided it equally among the kings.
There were sixteen *nāḷis* in total, which were all the remaining relics;
at that time, he gave two *doṇas* each to the inhabitants of every city.
Having taken the relics, the kings, joyful and delighted,
went each to their own kingdom and had stūpas constructed.
Having taken a *doṇa* measure, Doṇa had the Tumba Stūpa built.
With joyful hearts, the Moriyas erected the Aṅgārathūpa.
One tooth was in the city of the Thirty-three Gods, one was in the city of the Nāgas;
one was in the realm of Gandhāra, and one belonged to the King of Kāliṅga.
In that context, who was Doṇa? At that time, he was the teacher of the assembly. While distributing the relics, he took one of the canine teeth and placed it within his turban.
Then Sakka, wondering "Who today shall receive the canine tooth relic?", looked into the interior of the turban.
Taking a jeweled casket, he went there with an invisible body, seized the relic, and departed for the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Having constructed a great stupa one yojana in height, he established it as the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya. Stepping upon it with the tip of his foot, he took one tooth-relic from the southern quarter.
At this point, the narrative of the Tooth Relic in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven should be understood as complete.
Then, the Nāga King named Jayasena, having heard that the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, thought: "Today is the last time to see him."
Thinking, "I shall go," he took the great wealth of the Naga king, went to Kusinārā, and performed a great worship.
Standing to one side, he saw the relic situated between the feet;

seizing it by means of his naga-magic power, he brought it to the naga realm and enshrined it in a jewel-encrusted cetiya in the center of the naga city. This [relic] was [brought] to Tambapaṇṇi during the time of King Kākavaṇṇatissa.
The Elder Mahinda, a disciple of the Elder Mahādeva, went to the abode of the Nāgas, took a tooth relic, and brought it to Seru City in Tambapaṇṇi.
There, he had a Cetiya constructed between Giri and Abhaya in Seru City and enshrined it.
Up to this point, the account of the Tooth Relic from the Abode of the Nāgas should be understood as complete.
"Was this one from the land of Gandhāra? "One of the left-row teeth was taken by a teacher named Doṇa, having placed it within his garment.
At that time, a certain inhabitant of Gandhāra—who had previously received a prophecy and made a formal resolution—saw the tooth-relic placed within the teacher’s garment.
With a virtuous mind, he took the tooth-relic from there and went to his own kingdom together with the inhabitants of Gandhāra."
Having gone there, he placed it in the Cetiya Grove.
Up to this point, the account of the left canine tooth relic should be understood as complete.
Therein, the sage named Khema, a disciple of the Elder Sāriputta, [retrieved] the lower left canine tooth from the lattice-work basket itself.
Having flown up and seized the left tusk, he led it to Kāliṅgapura and went into the presence of King Brahmadatta.

Having shown the tooth-relic, he said: "Great King, the Blessed One has entrusted this very left tooth-relic to you in this Jambudīpa, so that it may work for the benefit of gods and humans through a succession of Guhasīvas, until finally it shall reach King Guhasīva."
"He brings" means he brought.
Later on, the princess Hemamālā, together with Prince Danta, assumed the guise of Brahmins, took the tooth-relic, and fled.
She informed the merchants, who traveled swiftly by ship; meanwhile, the *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas* performed a great worship [of the relic].
Having had [the city] constructed and traveling by stages, he reached the port of Jambukola; proceeding along the path pointed out by the eminent bird, he arrived at Anurādhapura.
Having inquired about the condition of Kittisirimegha and learned that he was nine years old and possessed faith in the Three Refuges, he went into the presence of the Great Thera Meghagiri.
After paying homage and sitting to one side, [he presented] the tooth relic.

Having announced that he had brought it from Jambudīpa, he showed it to him. Upon seeing it, his body suffused with joy, [the king] provided for both of them, adorned the Mahāvihāra, enshrined the tooth-relic of the Conqueror, and sent a monk to report these events to the king.
Hearing this, the king was filled with joy and gladness, as if he had attained the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti).
Like a poor man who, having seen his miracle and investigated it, became free from doubt and worshipped with the entire island of Laṅkā;
by this method of worship, he offered nine hundred thousand offerings in a single day.
The King of Siṃhala [offered] many jewels for both of them.
Having given sovereignty over the village and having bestowed his favor, he acted thus.
Up to this point, the discourse on the lower teeth-element should be understood as complete.
Forty even teeth, along with the hair of the head and the body, were taken entirely by the gods, one by one, throughout the succession of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
Regarding that speech, he resolved: "Let these forty even teeth, as well as the remaining teeth, the hair of the head, the hair of the body, and the nails—not burn when I have attained final Nibbāna;

let them be plucked out and established in the sky. And let each successive relic of hair, body-hair, nail, and tooth be conveyed to each individual world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), where, having had a shrine (*cetiyam*) constructed, they shall bring benefit to gods and humans. Therefore, from the time of his final Nibbāna...
As long as the body was not yet consumed by fire, the six-colored rays did not cease from the pores of his skin.

When the distribution of the relics was concluded, the Brahmin Doṇa, realizing that the relics had vanished from within his turban, his lower garment, and the space between his feet, fell prostrate upon the ground.
Then Sakka, the king of the gods, seeing this, [said]: "This teacher Doṇa..."

Thinking, "If he should meet with ruin after turning this for his own profit, I shall dispel his grief by assuming the guise of a lute-master and going into his presence," he cast off his royal form, took on the appearance of a lute-master, and went to him.
Standing to one side, he sang celestial songs and played the lute, uttering various kinds of inspired utterances. Whatever...
"This is the nature of things," he said, "that I shall cut off this man's argument. Having spoken thus, he spoke to those listening to the discourse:
"By destroying another's welfare through greed, a man becomes evil because of excessive greed. He illustrated this by citing the *Haṃsarāja-jātaka* and said, "What has been gained is well-gained.
Upon hearing this, Doṇa thought, "This lute-master has discovered my thievery," and was overcome with grief.

Having dispelled [his grief] and risen, as he was reflecting, he saw the urn; he realized that even the one by whom the Blessed One’s bodily relics had been measured was likewise destined for the relics.
Thinking, "I shall build a stupa here," he took the urn and placed it at the cetiya.
The Moriyas, taking the charcoal, built what is known as the Charcoal Cetiya.
In the city of Kapilavatthu, the majority of people possessed right view;
there they erected a reliquary stupa made of jewels.
In the delightful city of Allakappa, a portion of the Buddha’s relics was established.
He built a stupa containing relics out of stone the color of mung beans.
Having established the bodily relic in the kingdom of Pāveyya,
the people built the Pāveyya Cetiya out of stone the color of jewels.
In Madhurā, the great multitude honored his robe and alms-bowl;
in Kusaghara, they honored his lower garment;
in Kapila, his upper cloth; and in Kosala, his woolen blanket.
In Pāṭaliputta they honored the alms bowl and the waist-band;
in Avantī the sitting mat; in Campā the water-strainer;
in Devarattha the rug; and in Videha the water filter.
They also worshipped the razor and the needle-case at Indapatta;
the most excellent footprint at Pāsāṇaka; and the remaining relics at Parantaka.
At that time, the people honored the relics measuring eight measures (doṇas).
The relics of the Teacher, the Lord of the World, were distributed.
Those kings, having taken the relics obtained from themselves, went to their respective cities, had stūpas constructed, and performed great rites of worship.
The bodily relics of the Blessed One Cakkhumant amounted to eight *doṇa*s.
Was there one hundred and twenty-eight *nāḷikas* [of gold] in the golden tube?
The Teacher, however, took conception in his mother’s womb under the constellation Uttarāsāḷhā; he emerged from his mother’s womb under the constellation Visākha;
he went forth on the Great Renunciation under the constellation Uttarāsāḷhā; he became a Buddha under the constellation Visākha; and under the constellation Uttarāsāḷhā...
He set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. By that same [constellation], he performed the Twin Miracle.
Under the constellation of Assayuja, he descended from heaven. Under the constellation of Visākha, he attained Parinibbāna.
The two great elders, the Thera Mahākassapa and the Thera Anuruddha, having caused the relics of the Blessed One to be distributed, gave them away.

When those kings had obtained the relics of the Blessed One and, after performing a most precious worship for seven years, seven months, and seven days, had departed, the people of wrong view said regarding the Perfectly Enlightened One: "The ascetic Gotama has attained final Nibbāna;
he is performing this worship by destroying our livelihood for the sake of his relics."
“They are becoming corrupted. Sakka, perceiving this and knowing the reason for it, informed the Elder Mahākassapa:
“Venerable sir, people with wrong view who die here with a mind corrupted toward the Blessed One are reborn in the Avīci hell.
In the future, there will be many kings with wrong view who will be murderers of their mothers and fathers. This very day, the relics...”
"It is fitting to enshrine [the relics]," the Elder reflected, and then he saw [the truth].

Having accomplished infinite benefit for sentient beings during his lifetime, he—possessing a heart free from dejection—left behind his bodily relics for the sake of those remaining and entered the jaws of death.
(Having fulfilled the perfections in order to awaken to the various supreme powers of the knowledge of enlightenment...)

Having spoken thus, after traversing countless immeasurable existences, he swiftly ascended to the noble, auspicious state—the deathless, cool condition—and reached the further shore of birth, having accomplished what is difficult to do: the total burning away of all states of existence.
Seeing an obstruction to the elements, the Elder named Kassapa—
"Make a repository for all the relics," he said to the king.
Having assented with "So be it," the King of Māgadha, his mind delighted,
had a repository for the relics constructed everywhere, including the enclosures and other structures.
Having had [the stupa] built, the king informed Kassapa;
the Elder brought forth the relics, seeing this reason:
the serpents had taken possession of the relics at Rāmagāma.
In the future, they will maintain the cetiyas on the island of Laṅkā.
Having deposited those relics, the elder named Kassapa then gave the relics to King Ajātasattu.
The king placed those sixty-four hundred reliquaries inside; all those relics of the Buddha were deposited there.
It was adorned with eighty caskets and embellished with eighty cetiyas.
Having had a vast area, measuring the extent of a stupa-precinct,
thoroughly leveled, he had it covered with sand and scattered thousands of various flowers and diverse perfumes there.
He had eighty thousand forms of the Elder Asīti,
eight hundred wheels, and the form of King Suddhodana, as well as those of Māyā,
Pajāpatī, and others— all these forms he had fashioned out of gold alone.
The lord of the earth raised up five hundred parasols and banners.
Around each golden jar and each jar made of jewels,
he had exactly five hundred jars placed on every side.
The Lord of the City had five hundred lamps each placed in bowls made of gold and silver, having caused them to be filled with fragrant oil and set alight. He established them in this manner.
The Great Sage resolved that these [teachings] should remain exactly as they were:
"In the future, Dhammāsoka shall cause the teachings to be expanded.
Thus, the one of great intelligence had them engraved upon golden plates.
Having planned a miraculous feat all around the relic chamber,
he had a mechanical figure fashioned that could travel with the speed of the wind.
Having constructed a stone enclosure and sealed it with stones, he—
Upon that, he constructed a stupa with a stone base, level [with its surroundings].
The account of the enshrinement of the relics is complete.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Section on the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata," in the *Dhātuvamso* composed for the purpose of inspiring faith in the noble ones.

3. Discourse on the Succession of Relics When the relics were being distributed after having been divided among the various groups, the Teacher’s forehead relic fell to the lot of the Mallas of Kusinārā.
The Elder Mahākassapa approached them and said, "The Teacher’s forehead relic is in your portion."
"He came to take it; for while the Blessed One was still living, he authorized Tambapaṇṇidīpa [Sri Lanka]. Therefore, give it to us.
Hearing this, the Malla kings said, "Venerable sir, please accept the relic," and they gave it to the Elder Mahākassapa.
He summoned his own pupil, the Elder Mahānanda, and [placed] the forehead relic upon the elder's head.

"Having entrusted this relic, [he said: 'In the island of Tambapaṇṇi, on the southern bank of the Mahāvālukagaṅgā, at the edge of the lake named Seru, upon the snout of the boar named Varāha, a king named Kākavaṇṇatissa shall establish it;
he shall cause a cetiya and a monastery to be built. You, taking this relic, [should place it] in the Mahāvana Monastery near Vesālī."
Having placed [the relics] in the fragrant chamber where the Teacher had dwelt in the gabled hall, and having performed a worship of the relics,
when the life-force was relinquished and he was passing into final Nibbāna, he recounted the lineage of the relics to his own co-resident,
the Elder Candagutta, saying, "Be diligent! Having given the relics to the Elder, he passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.
That disciple, who was like the Teacher himself and possessed the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā),
took the relic and honored it with great joy in the Great Forest (Mahāvana).
The Elder Candagutta, a co-resident disciple of that Elder, took the relic and, having ascended into the sky, [arrived] at Sāvatthī.

Having established [the relic] in the Gandhakuṭī where the One Possessed of the Ten Powers had dwelt in the Great Monastery of Jetavana, he performed worship to the relics and remained there for a long time.
When his own life-force was exhausted and he was about to attain final Nibbāna, he summoned his co-resident, the Elder Bhaddasena,
entrusted the relic to the Elder, recounted the lineage of the relics, and having given him instructions, [passed away] into the realm of Nibbāna without residue.
He attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna.
The greatly wise Candagutta, possessing the six supernormal powers and full of confidence,
placed his relics in the delightful Jeta Grove and paid them homage.
His disciple, the Elder Bhaddasena, took the relic and traveled through the air to the Mahāvihāra at Isipatana, the Place of the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Having placed it in the Perfumed Chamber where the Teacher had resided, he worshipped it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and dwelt there for a long time.
When he was about to attain final Nibbāna, he entrusted the relic to his own co-resident, the Elder Jayasena.
Having entrusted [the relics] and recounted the history of the relics, he attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
The great elder Bhaddasena, who had fulfilled his duties and was a great seer,
established the relic at Isipatana, paid homage to it, and passed into extinction.
Then, having taken that relic and placed it in the Perfumed Chamber where the Teacher had dwelt in the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana,
and having worshipped it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, the Elder Jayasena lived there for a long time. When he was about to attain final Nibbāna,
he entrusted the relic to his own co-resident, the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita, and after recounting the history of the relics, [he passed away] into the Nibbāna without residue.
He attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna.
Having taken the supreme relics, the great sage Jayasena enshrined them in the delightful Veḷuvana grove and performed a beautiful worship.
Then the Venerable Elder Saṅgharakkhita, having taken the relic, traveled through the air and arrived at Kosambī.
He enshrined it in the Fragrant Chamber where the Blessed One had resided in the Ghosita Monastery, which had been built by the merchant Ghosita;
there he dwelt for a long time, making offerings of perfumes, garlands, and other honors. When he was about to attain final Nibbāna, he [entrusted] his own co-resident, the Elder Mahādeva...
Having summoned [the people] and recounted the history of the relics, he said, "Be heedful! and then passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue.
The Elder named Saṅgharakkhita was as clearly manifest as the moon;
having established himself at the Ghositārāma, he performed a delightful act of worship.
The Elder Mahādeva, who was the co-resident disciple of that Elder, took the relic and,
at the time when the white parasol was being raised for the sub-king Mahānāga— the brother of the great king Devānampiyatissa— at Mahāgāma,
he descended from the sky and sat down at the foot of a great *sāla* tree in the region named Hatthoṭṭha, between Kukkuṭapabbata and [the other mountain]. At that moment, Mahākāḷa...
The lay follower named [Name], together with his wife and children, had them take flowers, perfumes, ointments, banners, flags, and other offerings;
he remained for a long time, carrying the relic three times a day with grand ceremonial rites.
On the eight Uposatha days of the month, six-colored rays of light issued forth from the relic. At that time, that place...

It was as if it were the time when the Buddha was still living. The people dwelling in the countryside also took up the precepts in the presence of the Elder, observed the Uposatha, gave alms, and performed great worship at the Cetiya.
Later on, while residing in Mahāgāma, the viceroy caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming: "Whoever [offers] our Relic of the One Possessing the Ten Powers..."
"Having taken it, I have come here; I shall grant him great prosperity.
At that time, the householder Mahākāḷa, thinking "I will see the viceroy," took suitable gifts and stood at the palace gate, sending a message.
The viceroy had him summoned. He went, paid homage, and stood there, [presenting] those gifts to the king's men.
He concealed it. "The Viceroy? [Mahākāḷa replied,] "Uncle Mahākāḷa, there are relics of our Teacher in your kingdom.
When Mahākāḷa heard the Viceroy's words, he said, "There are, Your Majesty.

From my own preceptor, the Elder who is my spiritual friend, I have [received] a relic from the Teacher’s forehead, the size of a mirror-disk, which, with its six-colored rays, [illuminates] the expanse of space like a thousand suns and a thousand moons."
"It shines as if it were the time of sunrise. That country was like the time when the Buddha had appeared," he said.
As the householder heard these words, the king’s entire body became filled with five-colored rapture (*pīti*).
Overcome with extreme joy, the king [gave] one hundred thousand *kahāpaṇa* coins to his maternal uncle, Mahākāla.
"Give him a chariot yoked with four horses, well-adorned with golden ornaments, one horse, a field in a place convenient for water,
and five hundred female slaves," he said, and granted him other favors as well. Having caused this much to be given to the householder,
the viceroy had the drum beaten throughout the city on that very day and provided elephants, horses, chariots, and palanquins.
Having taken the householder and made him his guide, he gradually reached the province of Hatthoṭṭha.
Having established his camp in a delightful location on the ground, surrounded by his assembly of ministers and taking the householder with him, he went to the Elder’s dwelling place.
After paying homage, he stood to one side. The other ministers and the householder likewise [paid homage] to the Elder.
Having paid homage, they stood to one side. The viceroy, having paid homage to the Elder and engaged in friendly conversation, sat down to one side and exchanged greetings.
The Elder Mahādeva, having likewise engaged in friendly conversation, said:
“For what purpose have you come here, Great King? Tell me the reason for your visit. “Venerable sir, it is to be in your presence that we have come.”
"It is said that there is a relic of the Blessed One’s forehead-bone. I have come here thinking, 'I shall pay homage to it,'" he said.
The Elder replied, "Excellent, Great King, what you have done," and having opened the door of the relic chamber, he said, "Great King, the Buddha’s forehead-bone relic is exceedingly rare.
Having bathed with sixteen vessels of scented water and adorned himself with all his ornaments, the King [entered].
Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and raising his joined palms in reverence, he stood there paying homage.
His entire body was suffused with the joy inspired by the Buddha as his object of focus.
(Driven by the force of that joy, the king spoke these verses:)
I bow at your feet, O Hero, beautiful with the auspicious wheels upon their soles;
you who are worshipped by gods and men, grant me the deathless state when worshipped.
O Lord of the World, you alone are the refuge for all living beings.
In the world there is no one equal to you; deliver the vast multitude of people!
O Bhante, we are submerged in the great ocean of long-standing existence;
without refuge and without support, we have wandered there for a long time.
"Now you have reached a firm foundation;
having paid homage to you, we have crossed over the ocean of existence.
At that moment, rays of light issued forth from his relics, and the entire island of Laṅkā was covered with streams of golden liquid.
It was as if he were seeing it directly. Great joy and gladness arose within him. Having attained great gladness, the king became delighted and elated.
Emerging from the relic chamber, he sat down to one side together with the Elder in the decorated pavilion.
As he sat to one side—having avoided the faults of sitting, namely: too far away, too near, too high upwind, too high a place, facing directly toward [the Buddha], or too close behind—[he spoke].
If one is sitting too far away, one must speak in a loud voice if one wishes to speak. If one is sitting too close, one creates a disturbance.
If one is sitting upwind, the odor of the body wafts toward [the teacher]. If one is sitting on high ground, one displays disrespect.
If one is sitting directly in front, one must look by meeting eye-to-eye. If one is sitting too far behind...
"Sitting, one must look by turning the neck. Thus, sitting while avoiding the faults of such a posture," he said.
"Venerable Sir, give this relic to me. Having performed great honor and worship, I shall carry it away. "It is auspicious, Great King;
even while the Perfectly Enlightened One was still living, he made a prophecy concerning this relic. In your lineage..."
"A king named Kākavaṇṇatisso will be born on this island;
on the southern bank of the Mahāvālukagaṅgā, at the edge of the lake called Seru, he will establish [the relic] upon the head of an elephant named Varāha and build a great stūpa.
Having said this, the Teacher entered a meditative attainment there and, together with five hundred arahants, [repeated this] three times.
Having performed a circumambulation, he departed. Therefore, "Take it, O Great King," he said, and gave him the relic.
The king, having taken the relic and placed the relic-casket upon a square couch, set the relic within the casket;
then, having mounted it upon a chariot yoked with auspicious Sindh horses resembling white lotus petals, he established a guard all around it.
Having made an agreement (the King, having taken the relic), he sent word to the great multitude, saying, ‘Let him come later while we cause the fourfold army to be mobilized.
Then, having gone into the presence of the Elder Mahādeva, he said, ‘Venerable Sir, please come along to pay homage to the relic. Having heard his words, the Elder said, ‘Great King, this relic—’
"It has come down through succession. Like the Venerable Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma for the Blessed One, I shall preserve this relic.
Having said this, he took leave of the householder who was his provider of requisites, and taking his bowl and robes, he followed closely behind as the relic was being carried along.
The King, having taken the relic, eventually reached Mahāgāma and [sent for] Mahāsenagutta.
"Having summoned him, have the city decorated," he said. He, having caused the drum to be beaten throughout the city, commanded:
"Sweep the eighteen streets; set out full water-jars; hoist flags, banners, and the like;
erect archways; scatter flowers of five colors; decorate the entire city; and taking perfumes, garlands, and so forth..."
He gave orders that all the people of Nāga should come out to meet him with their upper robes draped over one shoulder.
Then the great multitude set out to meet him, sounding all kinds of musical instruments and carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands.
The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen were immeasurable in number. [The city was] strewn with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and filled with full water-jars and raised banners.
The assembly raised thousands of shouts of acclamation. Like the roar of the ocean struck by fragrant breezes, the entire city was filled with a single sound.
That king, having said, "Let all beings in the prisons of the city be released from their bonds;
let [the king] rule according to Dhamma and with justice," took the relic, entered his own city, and went to his royal palace.
Having arrived, they gave a signal to the musicians, saying, "Worship the relic. Adorned with various ornaments,
the musicians emerged from the royal palace, paid homage to the relic,
and carefully taking up the musical instruments held in their hands, they performed a great offering.
Then, having summoned a carpenter, he had a relic chamber constructed on a level ground not too far from and not too near the royal palace;
having established floral and vine-work decorations and the like, and having caused a variegated pavilion to be built within the relic chamber,
he had a relic casket made of the seven precious gems, placed the relics within that casket, and [prepared] a jeweled throne.
Having placed the relic upon his head, he had a variegated canopy fastened above it and surrounded it with a screen of cloth;

then, with a great retinue, he performed a grand worship of the relic. Great crowds of people, taking perfumes and garlands, performed a great worship of the relic on the eighth day of the Uposatha within each month.
Rays of light burst forth from the relic, and the great crowds were filled with wonder.

They gave shouts of approval. Overcome with joy, all the inhabitants of the city took up the rapture directed toward the Buddha and spent their days performing great worship of the relics day after day.
They observed the five precepts and, becoming devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, they went for refuge. The king [acted] for the sake of the great multitude.
He exhorted them, saying: “Cultivate loving-kindness; cultivate compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

perform the duty of honoring those who are senior in the family. Having thus exhorted them, he bestowed a great almsgiving upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, like the time when a great flood sets forth from the Ganges.
Standing in the place of mother and father, he sustained the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The great masses of people...
Abiding by his advice and performing meritorious deeds such as giving, most people who died during that time went to heaven.
People established in the section on the virtuous always performed meritorious deeds such as giving.
All people, having been liberated, with joyful minds, have gone entirely to a happy destination, delighting in the auspicious.
The king, performing great worship for the relics, resided in Mahāgāma. Should the monasteries established by him be mentioned?

How so? Having established monasteries such as the Lenavihāra, Candagirivihāra, Koṭipabbatavihāra, Nagaraṅgaṇavihāra, Selakāvihāra, and Talākāvihāra, he offered the water of dedication to the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahā-Ariṭṭha and dedicated them to the Mahāvihāra.
Thus that king, having maintained the relic for as long as he lived, [passed away].
In his final hours, lying upon his deathbed, he summoned his son, Prince Yaṭālatissa, and said:
"Dear Tissa, worship the forehead relic that we have preserved. Having thus related the history of the relic and instructed his son, he passed away and went to the city of heaven.
The king, a preeminent great nāga of great renown and wise,
having ruled the kingdom with true faith,
honored the Saṅgha with the four requisites.
Agā passed away to the excellent world of the gods.
His son, Prince Yaṭālatissa, after the passing of his father, performed a great worship of the relic in accordance with the very regulations established by his father.
He too, ruling the kingdom for a long time while performing the meditation on the relic three times each day, [passed away].
He dwelt there. By this, the monasteries he established should also be mentioned:

having established the Dhammasālavihāra, the Mahādhammasālavihāra, the Selābhayavihāra, and others, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Mahā-Abhaya—the preceptor’s pupil (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Tipiṭaka-Mahā-Ariṭṭha—was the grandfather of the Viceroy Mahānāga. He gave [the relic]. That king, too, having preserved the relic for as long as he lived, at the final time when he was lying upon his deathbed, summoned his son, Prince Goṭhābhaya, and said, "Be diligent in performing great worship for the relic.
Having thus spoken and related the lineage of the relic, he passed away and was reborn in heaven.
The great lord of the earth named Yaṭṭhālaka,
a refuge of virtues who acted for the welfare of the multitude,
performed extensive and manifold worship of the relics.
Having performed this, he went blamelessly to the city of the gods.
His son, Prince Goṭhābhaya, after his father’s passing, performed a great worship of the relic according to the very same regulations prescribed by his father;
then, having become King Goṭhābhaya and ruling the kingdom, [he encountered] ten brothers who were kings in the village of Kācara.
Having had them executed for the purpose of punishment, [he confiscated the following monasteries] from the Mahāthera Goṭhābhaya,
who resided in the Hatthadha-janapada: Mattikaleṇa-vihāra, Khīrasāla-vihāra, Nāgamahā-vihāra,
Kumbhasela-vihāra, Cetiyapabbata-vihāra, Sānupabbata-vihāra, Kaṇikārasela-vihāra, Ambasela-vihāra, Tiṇdukaleṇa-vihāra, Karaṇḍaka-vihāra, and Godhasāla-vihāra.
Having caused one thousand monasteries to be built— five hundred on the opposite bank of the Gaṅgā, such as Vālukatitthavihāra and others, and five hundred on this side—
he offered the water of dedication to the Elder Goṭhābhaya, whose name was identical to his own, and gave them to him.
Having performed worship of the relics for as long as he lived, at the end of his life, lying upon his deathbed, he [addressed] himself...
Having summoned his son, Prince Kākavaṇṇatissa, and embraced him, the Teacher said:

"Dear Tissa, this forehead relic has come down to us through our lineage. You, it is said, shall take this relic and, on the bank of the Great Gaṅgā at the edge of the mountain named Seru, establish it upon the head of a boar statue named Varāha, and there cause a monastery to be built."
While still alive, he made a prediction: "Therefore, after my passing, you must take this relic and enshrine it in that place.
Having thus instructed his son, he passed away and was reborn in heaven.
Then there was a lord of the earth named Goṭhābhaya.
Being diligent, he pleased the great multitude;
having performed extensive worship of the relics,
he went, free from sorrow, to the excellent world of the devas.
Mahānanda, of great wisdom, Candagutta, the learned;
the Elder Bhaddasena, confident in the auspicious Dhamma;
and the hero Jayasena, that Elder Saṅgharakkhita.
The elder Deva was wise, and the protectors of the relics were auspicious.
There was the sub-king Mahānāga, Yaṭṭhālaka of great strength,
Goṭhābhaya of great merit, and Kākavaṇṇa, who was full of vigor.
These elders and kings were meritorious and of noble mind;
they were experts in the relics, having brought forth the lineage of the relics.
These [relics] had come down through the succession of elders beginning with Kassapa.
From Mahānāga onwards, until [the relics] reached Tissa.

His father brought a girl home and established her as his son’s wife in the house. Later on, his father passed away.
The youth became known as “Caraka. From that time on, he attended upon the Paccekabuddha.
Caraka planted plantains, breadfruit, and other trees on his own residence site and established a fruit orchard.
Later on, a breadfruit tree planted by him produced a breadfruit as large as a great jar. Caraka [tended] his own residence...
Having gone there, he saw a perfectly ripe jackfruit on a branch; he cut it down, brought it home, removed the husk from its support, and set it down.

Then, as if fourfold sweetness were flowing out, the juice descended, and when the support was removed, it stood filling the hollow. Thereupon, Caraka thought: "This jackfruit belongs to our Paccekabuddha."
Thinking, "It is not fitting for others," he set it aside after putting it in order.
On the following day, the Paccekabuddha emerged from his cave, attended to his body,
and having put on an inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) as red as a fresh sprout and arranged it evenly all around, he donned a thick, excellent *paṃsukūla* robe.
Holding a bowl the color of a blue bee in his hand, he arrived through the air and appeared at the door of the hut.
Caraka emerged from the hut, paid homage to him, took the bowl from his hand, led him into the house, and had him sit on a seat.
Then, taking a jackfruit from the place where he himself kept them, he filled the bowl with juice.

Then one day, as Caraka was departing for another country, he summoned his wife and said, "Mother, give alms to the noble one with diligence," and having entrusted all his belongings to her, he went abroad. On the following day, the Paccekabuddha...
Having emerged from the forest, put on his robe, and taken up his bowl, he came through the air and descended at the door of the hut,
