When he had finished his meal, she saw the young paccekabuddha and, conceiving a mind associated with defilement, spoke her own desire to the paccekabuddha.
Having heard her words, the paccekabuddha felt disgust; he rose up and departed through the air back to his own dwelling place. She [then addressed] the paccekabuddha...
When the time had come, she smeared her body with oil and lay down on the bed groaning like one suffering from a disease.
When the physician arrived from another country and saw his wife lying there, he said: "My lady, did you give alms to the noble monk?
Groaning, she replied: "Do not ask about your noble husband’s karma. Tell me, my lady, what [did he do]?"

"By him the deed was done. He strove to gain an opportunity for himself along with his defilements and passions, but when I said, "This is improper," he seized me by the hair, beat me with his hands and feet, scratched my body with his nails, struck me on the head, and departed.
When the wandering ascetic heard this, unable to endure it, [he thought], "He has committed such an unmonastic act against me..."
Having said, "I shall wait," and having dispelled her grief, he took up his bow, seized a sharp arrow, and saying, "I will kill this man and return," he went to his dwelling place.
At that time, a Paccekabuddha had gone for the purpose of bathing. Having gone there, he [placed] his waist-band in the air...
Having arranged his lower and upper robes like a robe-stand and placed them upon it, he put on a water-silk garment, sat cross-legged in mid-air above the water, and began to bathe.
The Caraka, perceiving the reason for the Paccekabuddha’s profound reverence, stood hidden within a thicket.
Standing there, having witnessed such a marvel, he thought: "And this..."
"She does not do such a thing; surely she is speaking a lie. Having accepted her words, I committed an offense against this ascetic without cause.
Thinking, "He does not do such a thing," I went while the Paccekabuddha was standing after bathing, fell at his feet, and said, "Venerable sir, forgive me. The Paccekabuddha—
“What were you saying, lay follower? He explained what his wife had said.
“If that is the case, lay follower, it is fitting for you to go after finishing the business for which you came,” he said. “Do not speak thus, master!
Out of ignorance I accepted her words and have come to cause you trouble for no reason,” he said, recounting everything.
She explained what she had thought to herself.
“Was it a paccekabuddha? he asked. “Yes, lay follower,” she replied, “she spoke with me in conversation connected with what is not the true Dhamma.
He became angry at her and said, “Because of her, I have been offended by this man. I will go and kill her.”
Having paid homage to the Paccekabuddha with the fivefold prostration, she departed. The Paccekabuddha turned her back and,
after speaking many reasons why she must not kill the woman, established her in the five precepts and,
while teaching her the Dhamma, spoke this verse:
He who offends an unoffending man,
a pure person free from blemish—
the evil returns to that very fool.
“Like fine dust scattered against the wind.
Having heard his teaching of the Dhamma, Caraka became tranquil in heart; he paid homage with the fivefold prostration, went home, and lived in harmonious union with her.
From that time forth, for as long as he lived, [he served] the Paccekabuddha.
Having provided requisites such as robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick, he looked after him.
While dwelling in that very cave, at a later time, he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
Having penetrated the Dhamma through his own self-arisen knowledge—
Having abandoned all infinite suffering,
the illustrious and eminent one, delighting in concentration and jhāna,
has gone to destruction.
Then, later on, Caraka passed away and was reborn in the heavenly realm (*sagga*).

Having enjoyed celestial prosperity there for a long time, he fell from the world of the gods and was reborn in this island, in the kingdom of Malaya, as the son of Upacāraka, in a place near Amaruppala Lena.
He emerged from his mother’s womb at the completion of nine months and a half. On the day of his naming ceremony—
His relatives gave him the name Amaruppala Kumāra. Later, as he grew up, while playing with other children, he would cook sand-rice in leaf-bowls;

then, saying, "These children are ascetics," and having them sit down in a row, he would say, "I shall give alms," and thus bestow his play-offerings. One day, Amaruppala Kumāra [built] a sand-stūpa...
Having taken his own lower garment (*nivāsana-vattha*), he tied it to a small stick, fashioned it into a banner (*paṭāka*), and set it up for the purpose of worship.
Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving while residing at the Amaruppala Cave under the guidance of the Elder Maliyadeva,
when he passed away from there, he was reborn in this very island in the Mahāgāma village, in the womb of the chief queen of King Goṭhābhaya.
He took rebirth. At the conclusion of nine months and a half, he emerged from his mother’s womb.
On the day of his naming, they gave him the name Kākavaṇṇatisso. As he grew up in due course, upon the passing of his father, he raised the royal parasol and became the Great King Kākavaṇṇatisso.
As soon as his parasol was raised, the entire kingdom enjoyed an abundance of food.
It happened that for five or twelve days the rain fell properly without interruption.

At that time, at the almsgiving of the Bodhisatta Vessantara, just as alms-bowls were held in the hands of supplicants, the ponds, lotus-pools, rivers, caves, chasms, and mountain lakes became filled with rainwater.
They were covered with the five kinds of lotuses and crowded with many birds and various trees.
They became radiant. Various crops flourished, and there was a place for gems such as silver and gold, like the royal capital Ālakamandā in Uttarakuru.
That king, endowed with faith, provided the four requisites for the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus without deficiency, causing them to be given.
He had sixty masters of the Tipiṭaka sit down after filling a sandalwood trough with oil that had been processed a hundred times;
he then had them submerged in it up to their waists and feet.

He provided them with tooth-sticks made of rattan and *dhudanta* wood, along with the "four sweets," and gave them various kinds of snacks—sugarcane stalks, sugar lumps, coconut fruits, and root vegetables—to eat with fragrant rice grains.
And she gave him prepared *yāgu* (rice gruel) for his morning meal.

During the midday meal, she had various kinds of intermediate snacks (*antarakhajjaka*)—such as sugar cane, plantains, jackfruit, and other fruits—served together with fragrant *sāli* rice and diverse choice flavors;
and after the meal, she provided the eight kinds of permissible drinks (*kappiyapānaka*). She also provided other requisites for ascetics.
And he caused [it] to be given. In this very manner, he lived constantly bestowing great alms upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and upon the bhikkhus who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka.
Then, at another time, the great king Siva, in Kalyāṇī, [bestowed gifts] upon his own nephew, Prince Abhaya.
Having performed the marriage ceremony for his sister, the princess named Somadevī, King Kākavaṇṇatissa brought her back and gave her to Prince Abhaya as a wife.
Having given her away, he then established Prince Abhaya in Girinagara.
Ruling there in Girinagara, he became known as King Giriabhaya and enjoyed great prosperity.
He dwelt there. Later on, while the Great King Kākavaṇṇatissa was staying at Mahāgāma, he saw a boil that had arisen on the body of a certain bhikkhu at the spot where he had been bitten by a louse.

Seeing this, he asked, "Venerable sir, what is this? "It is a spot bitten by a louse, Great King. Upon hearing this, overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency, he asked, "Venerable sir, in whom do lice not exist?"

he departed. On that very day, while sitting in the water-shed, the Elder Tipiṭaka Tissa preached to the king the discourse called *Buddhasīhanāda*.
The king became devoted to the Elder; when an upper robe was being offered, [the Elder said], "I am one who wears but a single cloth."
Thinking, "I shall become [a king]," and thus reflecting, "It is not possible for me to give this away;
how then shall I act?", he stood right there on that upper terrace while conversing with the Elder. At that moment, a certain crow, perched upon a branch of a mango tree, cried out and spoke thus:
"Noble King Kākavaṇṇatissa, you have no doubt; at the moment of faith, give the upper robe to the preacher of the Dhamma."
“That crow, O protector of the earth, is capable of speech and speaks to you who have conceived faith in the Elder’s teaching of the True Dhamma:
‘Give your upper robe to the Great Elder.’”
"Great King, I have come having received five messages from you. First, Queen Vihāradevī has given birth to a son; this is the first message.
Second, a female elephant has given birth to a fine young male calf at the Tittha lake; this is the second message.
Third, a ship carrying seven hundred people has emerged safely at the port after passing through the midst of the ocean; this is the third message. [The fourth and fifth follow.]
At the foot of Mount Vaḍḍhamāna, in a field measuring two karīsas, golden shafts the size of the trunks of young palm trees rose up;

this was the fourth miracle. At the foot of Mount Giri, in the Koṭa-raṭṭhaka Monastery, the elder named Koṭa-raṭṭhaka, having spoken of the pacification of the path, rose to the height of seven palm trees upon the summit of Mount Giri and remained in the air.
Seated, he attained final Nibbāna; this is the fifth instruction.
(The son, the elephant, and the ship are the fourth, the section on the heap of gold;
the final Nibbāna of the Elder is this fifth instruction.)
Having taken this, I have come into your presence;
having heard such a message, take delight in meritorious deeds.
Give clothing immediately; all that was required has been assembled.
"Knowing this to be permanent, why are you preoccupied with your upper robe?
When the king heard the crow's words, he laughed. The Elder asked, "Why did you laugh, Great King?
[The king replied,] "Venerable sir, having heard the sound of the crow sitting within this mango branch and making a noise, I laughed. He related all of this.
The Elder, too, seeing the deed performed by the king in a previous existence, smiled. The king asked, "Venerable sir, why did you smile?
"Great King, I smiled because I saw the deed you performed during the immediately preceding existence in the kingdom of Malaya at the time called Amaruppala.
Being thus questioned, he explained in detail to him all the wholesome deeds that had been performed. The king—
Filled with joy, he gave his own upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) to the Elder, paid homage to him, and went home.
Having gone to the Koṭaraṭṭhaka Monastery, he had the Elder’s body cremated; taking the relics, he had a stupa built, performed a great worship ceremony, and then went to Mahāgāma.
Having gold brought, he had it placed in the royal courtyard. [He did this] within the belly of the ocean named Goṭha.
Having had cloths brought from his ship and caused them to be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus for the purpose of robes,
and having performed a great almsgiving, he built a monastery near Mahāgāma. While residing there,
he summoned his son Duṭṭhagāmaṇi and said, ‘Dear son, go and sit upon the mountain in the city,’ and appointed a minister to take his father’s place.
He sent him away, excluding Girinagara. Upon seeing him, Prince Giri-Abhaya provided clothing, food, and other necessities for the force that had come with the prince, and accorded him great honor.
The royal prince dwelt at the foot of the Giripabbata mountain.
Later on, a dispute arose among the kṣatriyas concerning their lineage. That King Abhaya thought, "What use have I for this dispute?"
Taking his army and vehicles with his wife Somadevī, he proceeded by stages and arrived at the presence of his ally Sīvarāja,
who was ruling in the city of Seru. Sīvarāja, for his part,
accorded a great reception to the force that had come with Giri Abhayarāja, and provided them with new garments, sesame seeds, rice, and other provisions.
Having had it brought, he had it given to him. After a few days had passed, [the king] asked: "My good man, why have you come?
He explained to him the entire reason for his arrival. [The king said: "Excellent, my good man! You have done well;

you have indeed come as one who ought to come. I shall know what must be done for you; do not worry. Having spoken thus, while searching for a site in the city for him to dwell in, [he found] a place at the edge of the lake.
Having seen that most delightful land, he established a city on that site and gave it the name Somānagara,
intending to give it a name identical to that of his queen. That city was highly prosperous, endowed with all necessary requisites such as wealth and grain,
and equipped with gates, watchtowers, city walls, moats, lotus ponds, and so forth, as well as with elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and the like.
The city became filled with a tumultuous clamor, crowded with the sounds of conchs, small drums, kettledrums, and other instruments.
For a long time, that Abhaya dwelt enjoying great sovereignty in the city of Soma.
Then, at another time, Queen Somā spoke with the king: "Noble sir, our refuge is the Cetiya."
"It is fitting to have a monastery built. Thinking, "What you have said is excellent," he became filled with joy.
While searching for a site for the monastery, he went to see a large *sāla* grove that was neither too far from nor too near the city.
At that time, in that *sāla* grove, there lived an elder named Mahāmahinda, who belonged to the lineage of the great Elder Ariṭṭha.
He was there, dwelling with about sixty monks. Seeing him and becoming inspired by his deportment, [the king] spoke thus to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, I shall build a monastery for you in this Sāla grove.
Having heard his words, the Elder consented by remaining silent. The king, filled with joy, paid homage to the Elder and returned to the city.
Having addressed Somadevī: "Bhadde Somadevī, our heart's desire has reached its fulfillment.
We have found a pleasing plot of land for the purpose of building a monastery. There, an elder named Mahinda dwells, having taken with him about sixty monks.
Having paid homage to him and obtained his consent to reside there, we have come. We shall build a monastery there."
He said. Having heard this, she was filled with joy and accepted it, saying, "Very well. On the following day, she went together with the queen to the presence of the Elder;
having paid homage, she sat down to one side. The Elder preached the Mahāsamaya Sutta to them.
Having both heard the Dhamma, they were filled with joy. Then the king asked, "Venerable sir, from where [did you obtain] the relic?"
Thinking, "We shall obtain it," he questioned the Elder. "Do not worry, Great King; we shall know where the relic is," the Elder replied.
From that time forth, he had the monastery grounds cleared, removing stumps, thorns, and other obstacles, and had them leveled until it was as beautiful and smooth as the surface of a drum-skin.
Then, having summoned a mason, he had a brick altar constructed and began the work on the cetiya.
He began the work. While constructing the cetiya, the carpenter completed the three flower-receptacles within a few days;
having finished all the work required for the relic chamber (*dhātugabbha*), he informed the king. The king came and reported it to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, the relic chamber has been completed. Having heard the king's words, the Elder [placed] the Tathāgata’s [relic], which he himself had been carrying...
