Having received the relic, the king—endowed with the virtues of faith and other qualities, and a protector of the world and the Dispensation—placed it within a relic chamber during an auspicious constellation and a favorable moment, accompanied by a great retinue, and had a most enchanting stupa constructed, resembling a mass of water bubbles or a crystal palace.
He was one perfected in the virtues of faith and the like, a guardian of the world and the Teaching.
The Great King had a monastery built as a shrine. Then,
having commissioned sixty monastic cells for the sake of about sixty monks in the presence of the Elder,
and having completed the monastery adorned with gate-towers and walls, he gave it the same name as his own queen.
Having offered the water of honor to the Elder Mahinda and performing worship with perfumes, garlands, incense,
and banners, King Giri-Abhaya went three times a day to attend upon the relics; while performing meritorious deeds such as giving alms and enjoying great prosperity, he resided in the city of Soma.
(In the delightful and enchanting city named Soma,
the Leader reigned, rejoicing together with his queen. Then one day,
the Elder Culla Piṇḍapātika Tissa, who was the brother of Queen Vihāradevī, [approached] King Kākavaṇṇatissa the Great.
Observing the life-force (*āyu-saṅkhāra*), he perceived that it would not endure for long. On the following day, he went into the presence of the king and spoke with him:
"Great King, the Teacher gave this prediction regarding the relic on your forehead:
'In the future, Kākavaṇṇatisso will appear at the head of a female boar named Varāha, at the edge of the lake called Seru, on the southern bank of the Mahāvālukagaṅgā.'"
"O Great King, he will establish my frontal bone relic," having said this, the Blessed One entered a meditative attainment and departed with reference to him.

"Pay attention to his words," he said. Having heard his speech, [the king thought], "Without destroying our store of merit, we must go for the purpose of having a cetiya built in honor of the Noble One's word."
Having agreed to the Elder’s words, saying, “Noble sir, it is well,” she summoned her own son, Duṭṭhagāmaṇi, from Girinagara and had him seated at Mahāgāma.
She then caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming:
“I shall have a cetiya constructed upon the head of a boar named Varāha, at the edge of the lake called Seru, near the Mahāvālukā Gaṅgā.”

"I shall go; let all the queens and the great multitude come with me. Having said this, the king went to the presence of the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa at the Tissamahāvihāra and the Elder Sāgala, and said:
"Venerable sirs, taking five hundred monks from among your retinue and attending upon the relics, please come along with me. Thus he spoke in the month of Bhadda.
On an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation and at a propitious moment, having prepared the royal camp, he brought the relic casket from the relic-house,
placed it upon a well-adorned chariot, held a white parasol over it, and had jeweled pavilions constructed ahead of it as it was sent forward.
Then the king, having summoned his son Duṭṭhagāmaṇi and instructed him, departed quickly taking with him Prince Saddhātissa and Queen Vihāradevī.
Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātiyatissa, taking five hundred bhikkhus from his own retinue, followed behind, attending upon the relic. And all the queens [followed] the king.
Having given a great alms-offering to the community of monks, they traveled together with the Saṅgha and reached Dīghavāpī.
Having seated Prince Saddhātissa there, they proceeded by stages until they arrived at the back of the Sumanamālā mountain, where he pitched his camp and sat down.
But why did that place come to have such a name? It was because for seven days the Nāga king Sumana...
While enjoying the prosperity of the Nāgas, he forgot the frontal-crest relic (*nalāṭadhātu*).
After seven days had passed, remembering the frontal-crest relic and subsequently reflecting upon it, he learned that the king had taken the relic and departed;
filled with great joy and possessing a great aspiration, he took his own retinue of about six million Nāgas and set out on the path back toward the relic.
In the very place where the Relic was established, a rain of jasmine garlands fell from the earth up to the height of a navel.
Therefore, that spot became known as Sumanamālāpiṭṭhi. On the following day, the King, taking the Relic, reached the place called Varāha.
Upon the arrival of the Relic at that spot, the Naga King Sumana [caused it to descend] as far as the hub of a chariot wheel.
Having caused it to sink, he made it unable to turn over. Seeing this, the king was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and questioned the Elder.
"Do not fear, Great King," the Elder said. "The Relic has come to the place where it shall be established;
it will be established in this very spot. Hearing this, the king thought, "This ground will become the site for the establishment of the Relic," and having encamped his army right there, he remained.
Having had the thorny forest cleared from all sides around this site and having had the ground made exceedingly beautiful and level like the surface of a drum, he addressed Seniya and his followers:
"First, you must have a relic chamber built for the purpose of enshrining the relics;
once the relic casket has been established within it, report back to me. The king [then entered] into that relic chamber inside the relic house.

Having established the relic casket and arranged for its external protection, he had a great ceremony of worship performed there and had the relic chamber anointed with the four kinds of fragrant scents. From that time on, that house became known as Gandhamūla.
Many people gathered at that place. There, the Elder named Mahinda [attended] to the visiting monks.
He performed his duties and services. On the following day, the king went to the monastery and, having asked, "Has the noble one lived in comfort?
he invited all the bhikkhus, seated them in the royal palace, and respectfully provided them with rice gruel and food.
Afterwards, while they sat listening to the expression of thanks for the meal, the Elder, giving them exhortation, said: "Great King, one should not live in negligence..."
"Life indeed is not long-lasting; therefore, without making a fuss, have the relic-shrine constructed. Having said this, he spoke the verse:
"For life is short and comparable to a bubble;
Therefore, a wise person should always perform wholesome deeds."
Having preached the Dhamma in this manner, the three elders— the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātiyatissa,
the Elder Sāgala, and the Elder Mahinda— each taking his own retinue of bhikkhus, came for the purpose of honoring the relics.
Possessing vast renown and bringing benefit to others...
"Benefiting the virtuous, steadfast, and possessed of unwavering faith,
well-encircled by a great assembly,
the best of kings began the construction of the magnificent stupa."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "Miscellaneous," in the *Dhātuvamsa* composed for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the noble ones.
5. Regarding the section on the depositing of the relics:
"Therefore, it is fitting to take possession of a plot of ground after having examined it.
While thus examining the site, he had eight oxen brought that were considered auspicious; he had them bathed with scented water and had golden breastplates fastened upon their horns.
Having caused the five-fingered mark of perfume to be given and having caused a garland and a chain of iron to be bound around his neck, did he think thus:
"If the relic of the Blessed One’s forehead, having established itself in whatever place and performing deeds for the welfare of the world,
shall cause the Dispensation to endure for five thousand years, then at that place the oxen shall themselves [be released] from the iron chain"?
Having left the stupa-veneration and wandered about on all sides, he resolved, "I shall sleep in the four directions," and gave orders to his men.
They did exactly as they were told. Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the king ordered the officials in charge of having the oxen brought back.
Those men went and, not seeing the oxen, reported to the king, "We do not see them, Your Majesty. "Go! [he said].
"Listen," he said, "look for the place where the oxen went. Searching for them, they did not see them at the place of tethering;
following the tracks step by step, they wandered all around the site where the cairn was being built.

Seeing the oxen lying in the four directions, they massaged their tails and other parts from where they lay, yet being unable to rouse them, they went and reported to the king: "Your Majesty, the oxen are not..."
"They have stood up; having wandered about one place, they are now lying in the four directions.
Hearing this, the king, though surrounded by his army, went there in person but was unable to make the oxen stand up. The king then made this resolution:
"If the relics are to be established in this place, let the oxen stand up and depart. The oxen—
They stood up and fled within a single moment of consciousness. Seeing that marvel, the king’s mind was filled with faith;
on another day, he had the horses adorned according to the same procedure as before, tied them with iron halters, and stationed them there.
Like oxen, those horses went and lay down. The king went there, made a resolution in the same manner, and caused the horses to stand up.
On another day, having had the elephant adorned, he made the same resolution.
That elephant also, having broken its tethering ropes, went immediately after the final watch of the night and lay down at the site where the Cetiya was to be built.
When the night had turned to dawn, the king summoned the elephant-keepers and said, "Bring the elephant. The elephant-keepers [went] to the place where the elephant was bound...
"Having looked, we do not see the elephant in its place of confinement, O King," they said. When he replied, "In that case, my men, search for it quickly!
the elephant-keepers, searching step by step, saw the elephant lying down at the site of the shrine (cetiya).
Having returned, they reported this to the king. Upon hearing this, the king acted according to the manner described above and arrived leading the elephant before him.
Having thus investigated him through these three modes of inquiry, he went into the presence of the Elder, paid homage, and while attending upon him, reported what had occurred.
At that time, King Siva of Seruna, having taken many gifts, arrived saying, "I shall see the King," and after paying homage, stood to one side. The King exchanged friendly greetings with him.
Having done so, while he was seated, the Great Naga King of the city of Loṇa also arrived, bringing many gifts, thinking, "I shall see the King.

He approached, paid homage, and sat down to one side. He exchanged friendly greetings with him and said, "In this place I shall establish a relic of the One Possessed of Ten Powers; you must be my companions."
"Take it and go; pay homage to the relic," he said, causing them to pay homage. At that moment, six-colored rays of light radiated from the relic.
The devas, uttering cries of "Excellent!", threw garlands down from the sky. The kings, filled with joy, exclaimed:
"The forehead-relic of the One of Ten Powers shall be established in our Laṅkā; this is our relic!"
Having paid homage with the thought, "May he accomplish the Teacher’s work for the great multitude," they departed.
When they had gone, the king summoned Giri-Abhaya and said, "Dear son, have the bricks made without causing oppression to the people.
"Do not worry, Your Majesty; I shall have the bricks made," he replied. "For if it were done in that way, there would be much delay," [the king] said. "As for us..."
When it was said, "Where shall we obtain gold and silver ornaments in such abundance?", Giri-Abhaya replied:
"Your Majesty, the Teacher is of great merit and will receive vast offerings, honor, and respect. Do not worry; you should begin the work on the stupa.
Having heard those inconceivable words from him, he was filled with joy and, having heard the Dhamma from the Elder, [acted accordingly].
Having paid homage to the relic and gone to the city, he ate his evening meal and, lying down upon his bed, fell asleep.
When the night had turned to dawn, he woke up and felt dejection as he was reflecting on the bricks.
At that time, Sakka, the king of the gods, addressed the divine son Vissakamma: "Dear Vissakamma, King Kākavaṇṇatissa is [troubled] by us..."
Having enshrined a relic from the Teacher’s forehead and desiring to have a great cetiya constructed, he thought of a brick and said, "Go and fashion a brick in a convenient place.
Hearing this, the divine son Vissakamma fashioned a brick in the field of a poor brahmin and returned to the world of the gods. At that moment, the owner of the field...
Early in the morning, a poor brahmin went to his field to inspect it.
While looking here and there, he saw a heap of bricks and thought, "Yesterday the king spoke of how he would obtain bricks.
Delighted, thinking, "I have indeed obtained a great gift," he took the bricks on a carrying-pole and went to see the king at the palace gate.
Having stood there, he sent a message. Having summoned him, the king asked, "Why have you come so early in the morning?
He replied, "Your Majesty, seeing a heap of bricks in my field, I came early this morning taking those bricks with me.
[The king] showed him that such bricks were suitable for the cetiya. Upon seeing them, the king was filled with joy and had much wealth bestowed upon the brahmin.
At that moment, another report was brought: "Four silver ships have departed from the port of Madanapaṭṭana, and four golden ships have set sail from Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
The chief guardian named Dhammapāla, who was stationed at the city gate, came and informed the king. Delighted, the king had the gold and silver brought forth.
Having brought together bricks, silver, and very costly gold,
he began the work on the cetiya.
By the power of the Teacher’s merit and by the strength of the king’s own merit, [the work proceeded].
"Everything thought of and contemplated is accomplished in an instant.
Then the king went to the presence of the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātiyatissa and said, "Venerable Sir, we shall go to the brick-making ground.
Having heard this, the Elder was delighted and, together with his own retinue of five hundred monks, went to the brick-making ground.
He departed. Then the Elder Mahāsāgalatthera and the Elder Mahindatthera went to the site of the brick monastery together with their own retinues of monks.
King Siva also went to the site of the brick monastery from the city of Siva. The Naga king also went to the site of the brick monastery from the city of Loṇa.
Giri-Abhaya, the king of Soma, also went to the site of the brick monastery, surrounded by his own military forces.
He departed. Because those ascetics, brahmins, and royal forces had gathered together, that stone slab became known as "Balavāhana" (the Powerful Carrier).
They all assembled at the brick ground. The Elder, looking at the heap of bricks, said this to the king:
"Great King, this heap of bricks is sufficient for all the work required for the cetiya. The king was delighted.
Surrounded by his army, he himself took the first brick. Seeing this, the remaining kings, the ministers and others, the assembly, and all the monks took bricks as well.
At that time, the king thought, "If I lift the burden and walk, it will cause a delay.
The Elder, knowing his mind, spoke thus: "Do not worry."
"Great King, take bricks and go. Afterwards, the gods, nāgas, and others will bring them, standing in an unbroken line from the brick-pit as far as the site of the cetiya.
Having brought them, they made a heap at the site of the cetiya.
Following that very same method, the gods, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others stood in an unbroken line until the completion of the cetiya.
Having brought bricks, they made a heap in each of the four directions at the site where the cetiya was to be built.
Then the king, having had all the bricklayers make a heap,
selected among those masons one named Jayasena, and gave him two garments worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
He caused a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas and ornaments such as golden earrings to be given.
He also caused all the necessary requisites, including new garments, to be provided for his retinue and the carpenters.
Having performed manifold great honors, he consulted with the Elder: "Noble sir, today is the Visākha full-moon Uposatha day; therefore—"
"Having performed an auspicious rite with the substance from the forehead, it is fitting to establish a brick at the site of the cetiya," he said.
Having heard this, the Elder replied, "Excellent, Great King! This is the day of the Blessed Buddha’s birth.
He then selected five men for the purpose of performing the cetiya construction: among them was one named Varadeva, one named Saṅkha, one named Vijja, and one named Pussadeva.

There was one named Mahādeva. Having had an auspicious ceremony performed for these carpenters, having dressed himself in festive attire and adorned with all ornaments, and having likewise adorned himself with every ornament, the king caused the auspicious rites to be performed;
then, having honored the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he circumambulated them three times and [stood] at the four...
Having prostrated at the various spots with the fivefold-limbed salutation and having performed the circumambulation, he entered the golden hall.

There, he had a son of a minister—who was adorned and embellished on both sides like his own living parents, and who was considered auspicious—take up a revolving staff inlaid with gold and composed of jewels, pearls, and gems;
and while that great shrine was being constructed there, he himself also...
Taking up his revolving measuring-staff and having traversed the ground that had been prepared, the great architect stood to one side.
Then, at an auspicious constellation and a favorable moment, he laid the foundation stone for the shrine.
At that instant, this great earth, extending over two hundred and forty thousand yojanas, gave a great shout of approval.

He let out a great roar as if he were moving along. Day after day, gods and humans provided enough clay for him to knead with his feet, and they gave it to him after sieving it through winnowing baskets.

Acting in this manner, within just a few days, he had constructed the three flower-receptacles and informed the great community of monks. Upon hearing this, the Saṅgha [appointed] two named Cunda and Uttara...
He commanded two novices, saying, "Go to the Himālaya mountains and bring back stones the color of fat.
Those novices were sixteen years of age by birth and had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) through the various sixfold super-knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*).

Having received the message from the Saṅgha of monks from the presence of the great Saṅgha of those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), they rose up into the air and [departed] from the Himālaya.
By means of their supernormal power (*iddhibala*), they brought stones the color of fat.
Having spread one of these stones upon the floor of the relic chamber (*dhātugabbha*) and fixed four stones at the four corners, they placed another stone to close the relic chamber,
setting it so as to be invisible.
Then the King, completing the work on the relic chamber, had nine crores of gold brought and given to the goldsmiths, commanding them:

"Make bricks for the relic chamber. Those goldsmiths made bricks that were one *ratana* in length, one cubit (*vidatthi*) in width, and four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) in thickness, and [constructed] the relic chamber.
They constructed it. Furthermore, having made that relic chamber sixteen cubits in height and ten spans by ten spans in width from side to side, they completed it using nothing but golden bricks.
In the center of the relic chamber, they had a Mount Sineru fashioned out of the seven precious gems;
upon Sineru, they fashioned the Pandukambala stone throne with natron-red lacquer and the Pāricchattaka tree out of the seven precious gems.
Having had a silver white parasol prepared by Brahmā, he had it held over the image of the Teacher.
At the foot of Mount Sineru, he had one hundred and eight rows of golden jars placed there, filled with fragrant paste and adorned with blue lotuses.
Immediately thereafter, [he had] one hundred and eight [rows of] silver jars, filled with fragrant paste and adorned with jewel-lotuses...
He had one hundred rows of jars set out. Immediately after that, he had one hundred and eight rows of jars made of jewels, adorned with white lotus garlands and filled with fragrant paste, set out.
Immediately after that, he had one hundred and eight rows of jars made of masāragalla stone, adorned with white lotuses and filled with fragrant paste, set out.
Immediately after that, [he had] one hundred and eight [rows of jars] made of ruby, adorned with campaka flowers and filled with fragrant paste...
He had rows of water-jars set up. Immediately thereafter, he had one hundred and eight rows of earthenware jars set up, adorned with five lotuses and filled with fragrant paste.
Between those rows of jars, he placed saucers made of the seven precious gems and filled with fragrant paste.
[There were also] golden [ornaments], saucers made of the seven precious gems, variegated garlands and creepers, full jars, the śrīvatsa, the nandyāvarta, the bhadrāsana, and so forth.

He also had constructed rows of elephants, horses, lions, tigers, bulls, and so forth. He commissioned the depiction of the Descent from the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Devorohaṇa*), the Twin Miracle (*Yamakapāṭihīra*), and others;
the subduing of Dhanapāla, Aṅgulimāla, Āḷavaka, and others; the Elder Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others;
and the forms of the eighty great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*). Furthermore, he had the central part of Mount Sineru fashioned, surrounded by the host of stars.
He had a moon disc made of silver fashioned, and he had a sun disc made of gold, adorned with a network of rays, fashioned.
Then, on the summit of Sineru at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, upon the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, he had an image of our Teacher fashioned out of solid, high-quality red gold;
[and he invited] ten thousand deities from the ten-thousandfold world-system, headed by the Mother Deity.
He had the Abhidhamma, consisting of the seven treatises, inscribed in the manner of a teaching.
Its twenty nails were made of ivory for the white parts of the eyes; the fingers, the soles of the hands and feet, and the lips were made of gold;
the red parts of the eyes were made of coral; and the hair, beard, and eyebrows were made of sapphire.
His forty teeth were made of diamond. His hair, however, was made of silver, possessing the splendor of silver bubbles set against a golden wall.
Above the Blessed One’s head, at the crown of his unblinking brow, they had a canopy fashioned of the seven precious gems, encircled by a network of variegated bells.
Inside the pavilion hung a beautiful cluster of pearls, worth nine hundred thousand [pieces of gold].

Having had a cloth canopy fastened, he had a net of pearls draped at the edge of the pavilion, and immediately thereafter, he had it surrounded by a net of tinkling bells variegated with the seven precious gems.

He also had an image of our Blessed One’s mother, the goddess Sujātā, fashioned out of the seven precious gems; likewise, he had images of the god Erāvaṇa, the divine artisan Viśvakarman, and others made.
And he caused Sakka, the king of the gods, together with his retinue, the four Great Kings,
the Gandhabba sons such as Pañcasikha, and the Great Brahmās such as Sahampati, to act [as the audience]. While composing the Vessantara Jātaka,
he [depicted] Saṃjaya the Great King, Queen Phusatī and her attendants, Queen Maddī, the two children, the Brahmin Jūjaka, and others.
He had [these] made: the Jātakas of Vidhura, Soṇadatta, Mahānāradakassapa, Sutasoma, Suppāraka, Saṅkhapāla, and others;
the modes of teaching such as the Dhammacakkappavattana and the Mahāsamaya Suttas;
and the Great King Suddhodana, Queen Mahāmāyā, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, Bhaddakaccānā the mother of Prince Rāhula, Prince Rāhula himself, Channa, and Kanthaka.
Having caused the Great Renunciation, the Great Seat of Enlightenment, the eighty great disciples, the great King of Kosala,
the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, Suppavāsā, and later Cūḷa-Piṇḍapātiya and the Elder Tissa, as well as herself, to be fashioned [in relief],
she enshrined them all within the relic chamber.
The description of the Relic Chamber is completed.
Having thus caused the worship arrangements for the Relic Chamber to be well-ordered and most pleasing, he conversed with the Elder:
"Venerable Sir, that which was to be done by me in the Relic Chamber has been finished. Tomorrow, under the Rohiṇī constellation, the relics shall be enshrined."
"I shall do so. However, the noble ladies are coming having taken the hair-relics. He placed the task upon the Elder Tissa.

Having heard this, the Elder said, "Excellent, Great King! We shall search for and have the hair-relics brought," and then, having summoned his own pupil, the Elder Siva, he said, "Friend, in the Bhūmindhara Nāga’s palace, there is one named Jayasena..."

A Nāga king dwells there, and near him are hair relics. Knowing the negligence of the two merchant brothers, Tapussa and Bhallika, at the time they were making offerings, the Nāga king took two hair relics and placed them in the Nāga realm.
He commanded: "Bring those relics and give them to the King. Having received this instruction, the Elder departed.
Then the king sent a message to his sister Somadevī and to his nephew Giriabhayarāja, saying:
"Tomorrow we shall perform the enshrinement of the relics. You must come bringing your military forces.
Having likewise sent such a message to Mahānāgarāja in Loṇanagara and to Sīvarāja in Seru-nagara, he himself also [prepared for the journey].

He caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming: "From this day forth, all of you, together with your retinues, must come to my victory, starting from whoever has received even as much as a single *karīsa* from my hand.
Hearing this, the great multitude, filled with joy, set out adorned and prepared according to their respective means. When dawn had broken, the king—
Having said, "At night all the guilds shall come to the deposit of the relics bringing perfumes,
garlands, incense, banners, and so forth," he gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; having given costly garments and other items for the sake of the three robes,
he himself, adorned with all his ornaments, ate various kinds of choice food, observed the Uposatha vow, and [donned] his jeweled earrings, girdle, and anklets.
Surrounded by dancing women resembling celestial nymphs, who were adorned with all kinds of ornaments such as bracelets and the like,
dressed in various fine garments of silk and other materials, and holding in their hands musical instruments for dance, song, and instrumental music,
he went to the shrine site together with those of the aforementioned description; there, having paid homage to the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he stood.

Then, in the city of Somanagara, King Giribhaya also had a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing that all the citizens should come to the place where the relics were to be enshrined according to their respective means.
Adorned with all his ornaments and surrounded by a well-prepared retinue of ministers, he set out.
Queen Soma, too, having bathed her head, dressed in new garments, and adorned with every ornament, appeared like a celestial nymph.
Like his own retinue, he had five hundred maidens dressed in blue garments and adorned in the same manner;

having had them take up full water-jars, immediately after them he had another five hundred maidens dressed in yellow garments and adorned in the same manner, and having had them take up articles for worship; and immediately after them, five hundred maidens in red garments...
Having dressed them in that same manner and adorned them, he had them take baskets filled with various flowers;
immediately after them, five hundred maidens were dressed in white cloths, adorned in the same way, and made to hold incense ladles.
Having thus arranged the ritual of worship, he went with his retinue to the monastery courtyard and [approached] the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having prostrated with the fivefold salutation and offered worship with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings,
she stood to one side together with her husband,
King Giribhaya. In the city of Loṇa, the Great Naga King was likewise adorned with all ornaments, surrounded by a circle of ministers well-prepared with every kind of finery.
Having had dancers, singers, and musicians perform, and having had incense, garlands, and censers brought, King Siva of Serunagara arrived at the site of the Cetiya;
there, after bowing to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he stood to one side.
King Siva himself, having adorned himself with all his ornaments, accompanied by a great retinue, [prepared] the ritual of worship.
Having caused [the relics] to be taken up, he came to the site of the cetiya, paid homage to the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and stood to one side.

The royal retinue, radiant with garments, ornaments, sandalwood, garlands, and the like according to their respective wealth, bound upon their foreheads variegated golden bands adorned with hanging clusters of pearls;
well-adorned and embellished with hand-ornaments and various other jewels, they resembled a celestial assembly.

Having taken up various weapons appropriate to their respective dress, they stood on one side. And having mounted an excellent chariot—which was adorned with the skins of lions, tigers, and leopards, decorated with golden ornaments, equipped with a golden banner, and covered with a golden lattice—charioteers, themselves embellished with every kind of ornament, stood on one side.
Sons of brahmins and others, wearing decorated hides and looking magnificent, stood on one side. Many ministers, each according to his own attire, [stood there].
Adorned with costly garments and ornaments, accompanied by their retinue, they stood to one side. Taking a right-spiraling conch shell filled with scented water,
arranging their upper robes over one shoulder, and binding on the brahminical head-dress, the brahmin household priests,
having had the ritual offerings prepared by a great retinue, arrived at the site of the shrine and [approached] the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having paid homage and proclaimed the sound of victory, they spoke thus:
"May the country always have security and abundant food, may it be auspicious;
may crops flourish, and may there be such victories for the king."
The rest of the great multitude spoke thus: "Let him dwell, surrounded by his ministers, upon this earth bounded by the ocean, girt by the sea, the bearer of wealth.

Having said this, they each, according to their own means, [prepared for the festival]. "Our noble lord, King Kākavaṇṇatissa the Great, shall establish the forehead-relic of the World-Chief, that One Person in the world including the devas! Thus they spoke.
Well-adorned and beautifully attired, even the hunchbacks, dwarfs, and all other people stood there holding offerings of worship and uttering shouts of "Sādhu!
This assembly gathered at the site of the cetiya should be understood as follows:
Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and merchants had assembled together, all carrying flowers and other offerings, and all were decorated with ornaments.
Countless and many great multitudes of kṣatriyas have gathered there like the spreading ocean; the great king,
adorned and surrounded by his royal retinue, has arrived.
Just as Sakka, the king of the gods, stood upon the courtyard of the cetiya,
the surface of the earth was filled with the cries of "Excellent! from the beings,
the sound of the fivefold musical instruments, and the noise of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātiyatissa, surrounded by his five hundred disciples who were all *khīṇāsavas*, arrived at the site of the Cetiya.
The Elder Mahāsāgalatissa also, surrounded by his five hundred *khīṇāsavas*, arrived at the site of the Cetiya.
The Elder Mahinda likewise, taking with him about sixty of his own disciples who were *khīṇāsavas*, arrived at the site of the Cetiya.
He arrived. In this very manner, as one, two, three, four, and five *khīṇāsavas* arrived, they eventually numbered about seven thousand.
Then, the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātiya-Tissa sat down on the terrace of the cetiya surrounded by so many bhikkhus.
Thereupon, the king approached, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and conversed with the elder. [Regarding] the hair-relics...
“From where shall we obtain it, noble sirs? At that moment, the Elder Tissa looked toward his own pupil, the Elder Siva.

At the very instant he was looked upon, the latter rose from his seat, adjusted his robe, paid homage to the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and—being one possessed of the six supernormal powers and a great destroyer of the taints—entered the fourth jhāna. Emerging from that, he [stood] upon the earth.
Having submerged himself, he appeared within the celestial palace of the Naga king who supports the earth.
(Upon hearing this, the Elder Siva, having attained mastery and being confident,
instantly became visible before the city of the Nagas.)
At that time, King Jayasena, the Naga king, surrounded by his own nephew and a retinue of two hundred million Nagas, was sitting there enjoying great glory.
Having given a sign by a gesture, and seeing the Elder approaching from afar, he thought:
"There is no business for recluses to perform in this abode of Nagas; without a doubt, it must be for the sake of a hair-relic."
Thinking, "He will come relying on me," he rose, entered the relic chamber, swallowed the relic casket, and sat down as if knowing nothing at all.
At that time, the Elder approached him. The Naga king went out to meet him and, performing the customary greetings, conversed with the Elder.
When asked, "For what reason has the Noble One come? he spoke thus:
When he said, "I have come for the sake of the hair-relics of our Fully Enlightened One, the Lord of the Three Worlds;

give me the hair-relics placed in your care without delay, for it was with reference to those very relics that we were sent by our preceptor," [the king] replied, "The hair-relics of our Fully Enlightened One are not in my possession. The Elder [then opened] the relic casket...
When he said, "O Great King, knowing that it has been swallowed, I shall take the hair-relics," [the king] replied, "Yes; seeing them, you may take them and go.
Having thus obtained his promise three times, and remaining exactly as he was, he then, by means of his psychic power (iddhi), fashioned a subtle thread.
Having placed it in his mouth,
he took the relic casket and emerged from the nāga abode, saying, "Stay, O nāgas! At that moment,
the nāga king Jayasena, having deceived the ascetic, said, "I have been sent," and departed when [the ascetic] had gone.
Having looked at the relic casket and not seeing the relics, [thinking] ‘I have been robbed by the ascetic,’ why do you stand with both hands raised,
raising a great clamor throughout your entire Nāga-abode and lamenting with a loud voice—
as if he had gone away after gouging out our very eyes, the Perfectly Enlightened One who is the refuge for the world including the devas?
"Let us follow that ascetic who has gone away after seizing the hair-relics, having overcome us who were not released from the suffering of the woeful states, and seize them ourselves!
Having taken two koṭis of nāgas, he followed behind his own nephew's back and rose into the air. At that moment, however, Siva Thera—
Descending from the sky, he entered the earth. Then they too entered the earth.
Thus, performing the miracle of emerging and submerging together with them, the Elder displayed his supernormal power and struck the Piṭṭhipāsāṇa rock not far from the city of Seru.
Having inspired them with a sense of spiritual urgency right there, he became manifest before the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the Cetiyaṅgaṇa.
Being unable to seize him, the nāgas let out a great cry and echoed it back.
From that moment on, thinking, "We are lost," they all gathered together upon that back rock and lamented with a loud voice, crying, "Alas, we are truly lost!
From then on, that back rock has continued to echo the cries of the nāgas.
Because of his lamenting and wailing, it was called Nāgagalla.
The nāga followed right behind the elder, went to the courtyard of the cetiya, and said to the king:
"Your Majesty, this bhikkhu has come having taken the relic that was not given by me. Hearing this, the king asked: "Is it true, noble sir, that the nāga..."
When it was said, "O Great King, did they not take the relic given by this [nāga]?
he replied, "The nāga gave you his testimony. The Elder made the nāga king Samaṇuppala the witness for his nephew.
Having heard all the words of that nephew, the king believed him. At that time, the nāga king was overwhelmed by suffering.
Having gone outside, he stood there. From that time on, because that Nāga king remained seated outside, he became known as Bahināgarāja ("The Outside Nāga King").
He, however, had his nephew sit within the courtyard of the Cetiya. Now, the Nāgas who took up the protection of this Cetiya must be mentioned:
the retinue of King Sumananāga consisted of about six koṭis of Nāgas, and [the retinue] of Jayasena...
The retinue of the Nāga King Samanu-ppala consisted of approximately one hundred million nāgas; the retinue of the Nāga King Samaṇuppala consisted of approximately two hundred million nāgas.

All of them undertook the protection of the relics. The king, having taken a hair-relic from the hand of the Elder and placed it upon a jeweled throne, gave it to his minister named Mahinda. At that assembly, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Mahāphussadeva...
The four novices who were his co-residents had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Among them, one was the novice named Sumanas, the son of King Malaya;
another was the novice named Uttara, the son of the nephew of King Siva from the city of Seruna;
another was the novice named Cunda, the son of a garland-maker from Mahāgāma; and the fourth was the son of a householder from Mahāgāma.
The novice named Mahākassapa said, "These four novices will today deposit the relics at the Mahācetiya under the great King Kākavaṇṇatissa;
we shall go to the Himavanta and bring back beautiful flowers.
Having paid homage to the Elder, they departed through the air for the Himavanta, gathered a worthy garland of campaka, nāga, salala, and other flowers, and went to the world of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
At that time, Sakka, the king of the gods, adorned with all his ornaments, having taken deities from two celestial realms and mounted upon the back of the elephant Erāvaṇa,
surrounded by a retinue of two hundred and fifty million goddesses, was wandering along the Great Sudassana Street;
seeing those four novices approaching from afar with their entire retinues, he [leapt] from the back of the elephant.
Having descended and paid homage with the fivefold prostration, he saw garlands and betel-boxes in their hands and asked, "Noble ones, what is this in your hands?
Upon hearing that, the novices said, "Great King, do you not know?
In Laṅkā, Great King Kākavaṇṇatissa took the frontal bone relic of the One Possessing the Ten Powers and, on the southern bank of the Mahāvālukagaṅgā, at the place called Seru..."
"Today, at the end of the Dāha mountain, he is depositing the relics after having had a cetiya constructed by the divine architect Vissakamma at your command, using bricks fashioned for that purpose.
This flower was brought from the Himālayas for the sake of worshipping there; we have come here to fetch more flowers," they said. Sakka—
Having heard their words, she said, "Noble sirs, having worshipped flowers in your hands at the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya, take flowers from our garden and go.
Having spoken thus, she went with them and worshipped the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya with those flowers. Then...

They informed Sakka that they must not engage in conceptual proliferation (*papañca*). Having heard this, Sakka had the novice monks take flowers from the five great gardens—such as the *pāricchattaka* and *koviḷāra*—as well as sandalwood powder, and sent them forth.
Taking the flowers, the novices descended from the world of the gods, entered the Himavat mountains, and [stood] in the cool shade near the golden jewel-mountain.
Having finished their meal and spent the day in seclusion, when the time for the evening stars arrived, they searched for the jewels and found four.
One was a sapphire (*indanīlamaṇi*), one was a radiant *jotiraṅga* gem, one was a beryl (*veluriyamaṇi*), and one was a *masāragalla* gem.
Taking these four gems and celestial flowers, they presented them to the elders.
"Thera? Your Majesty, these novices have arrived having taken with them flowers such as those from the Pāricchattaka and Kovilara trees, sandalwood powder, and four gems," they reported to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy; he paid homage to the novices by prostrating himself five times and took the gems they had brought.
Having taken [the relics] and given them to the minister named Mahānanda, he went with the elders and a great retinue to the Cetiyaṅgaṇa.

There, having taken the relics from the jewel casket and placed the relics upon his own head, and having caused a white parasol to be held over them, he circumambulated the Cetiya three times and stood at the eastern gate. This was for the One of Ten Powers.

He made this resolution: "May the relic of the forehead, having been enshrined upon the forehead of the Buddha image commissioned by us, appear in the form of the *uṇṇaloma* (the single hair-tuft between the eyebrows).

At the very moment of his thought, the relic rose from its casket into the sky, stood at a height of seven palm trees, and emitted rays of six colors. Those rays were like molten gold being poured from a ladle.

Like streams of molten gold poured from the sky, they seized the entire island of Laṅkā, making it one mass of light with their networks of rays. At that time, there was a miracle like the Twin Miracle.
Having seen this miracle never before seen even by the Blessed One, the Great Compassionate One, the great multitude felt as if they were directly perceiving the physical body of the Tathāgata.
Having witnessed a miracle of the Teacher never seen before,
the great multitude became filled with rapture and attained confidence in the Conqueror.
They each offered their own perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
All paid homage with their heads to such a sublime cetiya.
In that assembly, one wise man, praising the Jina, spoke thus:
"Even though the Buddha has attained parinibbāna, his glory remains such as this."
What kind of perfection belonged to the Lord of the World when he was established [in enlightenment]?
All this majesty of the Great Seer came through merit alone;
knowing this, one should perform merit, aspiring for supreme enlightenment.

At that time, people donned festive attire and took up various kinds of offerings—consisting of many types of worship, including a great and costly chariot variegated with diverse gems, adorned with numerous ornaments, with flags and banners raised high, and strewn with various flowers.
There was the sounding of many kinds of musical instruments. At that moment, the deities caused a rain of flowers to fall.

The Nāgas, endowed with great power, performed worship. Thus all the gods, Nāgas, and humans gave shouts of "Sādhu!", clapped their hands, and tossed up handfuls of dust; the elephants let out trumpeting cries.
The horses neighed with joy, and the thick, dense, great earth shook as far as the edge of the waters. Streaks of lightning flashed forth in all directions.
Throughout the entire island of Laṅkā, great trees such as the Sumanakūṭa were covered with clusters of flowers.
All the reservoirs were strewn with the five kinds of lotuses. Among the deities there were humans, and among the humans there were yakkhas, nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others.
There were immeasurable numbers of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. With a great cry of "Sādhu!"...
With a great roar, the entire island of Laṅkā became a single sound and a single resonance, like the ocean struck by a violent wind.
Having displayed this miracle of the relic amidst the assembly of the great multitude who were filled with serene confidence through this ritual of worship,
it descended from the sky and settled upon the forehead of the Buddha image, shining brilliantly as if surpassing the splendor of the full moon.
The king took a hair-relic from the hand of his minister named Mahānanda and, giving it to Queen Vihāradevī, said:
“You must place these hair-relics upon the head of the One Possessing Ten Powers, which has never been looked down upon.
She took the hair-relics and made this resolution: “May they be established right here! At that moment, the hair-relics [emerged] from the casket.
Rising into the sky, they emitted rays of light as blue as a peacock’s neck; descending from the air, they settled upon the head—the supreme limb—of the Buddha image.
Then the king, together with the Elder, entered the relic chamber, which was strewn with divine sandalwood powder and [flowers from] the Pāricchattaka, Koviḷāra, and other trees.
Having spread out a carpet of fragrant flowers, he placed four jeweled stones amidst a mass of radiant light.
The relic chamber, overwhelmed by their brilliance, shone exceedingly. All the female dancers removed their own ornaments and offered them as worship within the relic chamber itself.
Then the king, having performed the enshrinement of the relics for the Buddha image...
Placing his head upon the soles of [the Buddha’s] feet and lying down, he lamented thus:

"Starting from today, a separation has occurred between me and the relic passed down through my father and grandfather. Having stayed with you for far too long, I have now been brought from the delightful Rohaṇa country and established here.
Having said this, he became a great, blazing lamp upon the summit of Sineru.
"Are you as if standing right here? Now we shall not go; forgive us, Blessed One!"—thus lamenting, did he fall even within the relic-chamber and say:
"Alas! This suffering of separation oppresses me; these relics [are leaving]!"
Having spoken thus, lamenting, he then lay down in the relic chamber, saying:
"I shall die here; I will not go away, having abandoned my noble lord.
For me, wandering through saṃsāra, a sight of him is difficult to obtain."
Having spoken thus, he lay down lamenting. Now, within that community of monks, there was an elder named Sahadeva.
Seeing the king lying weeping inside the relic chamber, the elder surveyed his mind with the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), wondering, "What is his intention?
He perceived that the king had lain down thinking, "I shall die here," and [realizing this], through his supernormal power (*iddhi*)... the cycle of existence, which is so dear to him—
Having constructed it, he brought it out from the relic chamber.
(Having attained mastery through supernormal power, confident and possessing the six higher knowledges,
that wise one at that very moment brought the king outside.)
Then, having placed the first brought stone of *jotiraṅga* like a canopy over the relic chamber, [he said]:
"O Arahants, let the relic chamber become solid all around like a four-sided couch. Let the fragrances in the relic chamber not dry up;
let the flowers not wither; let the jewels not lose their luster; let the objects worthy of worship not perish."
They made this resolve: "May there be no opportunity or opening for our adversaries and enemies.

Then the King, having performed a great worship of the relics, completed the construction of the most enchanting four-sided enclosure at the Maṅgala Cetiya, as well as the parasol-work like the peak of Mount Kelāsa and the plaster-work starting from the base of sand, finishing all the work that was to be done.
Then the umbrella-bearer, white like the rays of the stainless moon, resembling a water bubble or a peak of Mount Kailāsa,
standing firm as a mountain, inspiring confidence in the virtuous, crushing those of other sects, shone like a stupa of auspiciousness.
He stood there, radiant, delighting the great multitude.
The Mangala-Kelāsa Stupa is immovable and well-established.
It inspires faith in the virtuous, crushes the views of the sectarians, produces confidence in those to be,
and is the most excellent source of serenity for all people.
The Cetiya, preeminent in the world and frequented by the great multitude,
shall always be worthy of worship, strewn with banners and flowers. Many people,
having gathered together from various lands, will assemble there.
They worshipped that Great Stupa at all times without weariness.
Such a suitable dwelling place is difficult to find;
therefore, O Lordless One, may there be much merit for those who are always heedful and peaceful.
The king wrapped the magnificent cetiya in fine cotton cloth, established the Great Bodhi tree named Sirivaḍḍhana, and there caused a Bodhi house to be built.
He also had a three-storied Uposatha hall constructed, as well as night-quarters, day-quarters, and so forth;
he thus performed everything that ought to be done for the monastery. Having had these things completed, he offered the water of dedication for the monastery.
Thinking, "I shall give," he offered a great almsgiving for seven days to eighty thousand monks, providing various kinds of soups and condiments; on the seventh day,
having had garments provided for the Triple Robe of the great community of monks,
and having eaten his morning meal at dawn, he went into the presence of the Elder, paid homage, and stood to one side.
“‘Venerable sir, I wish to give an offering to the Great Saṅgha of Bhikkhus on the fourteenth day. That venerable one spoke thus:
‘When the full moon is near, on the Uposatha day under the constellation Assayuja, it is auspicious to offer the relic.
Having heard the words of the Elder, he prostrated himself before the Elder with the fivefold greeting in the city of Somanagara.”
“Did you speak to your sister, the queen? My sister, I told the noble one:

‘Having enshrined the frontal bone relic of the One of Ten Powers at the Maṅgala Mahā Cetiya, I shall build a palace and a monastery with its gates, watchtowers, and archways adorned, and strewn with white cloth and many banners, and then I will offer the dedication gift.
But that venerable one, on the Uposatha day when the full moon was approaching—”
"It is proper to give," he said. "Your Majesty, what are you saying? Give the offering on the Uposatha day when the full moon is near, according to the noble sir's instructions," she replied.
Having heard her words, he was filled with joy and accepted, saying, "Very well, my dear.
While residing in Somanagara, as the Uposatha day of the approaching full moon arrived—
Knowing that it was the Uposatha day, he summoned Giriabhaya and said, "Dear son, tomorrow a sacrificial gift must be given;
you, having adorned your division of the army, come tomorrow with us. Having spoken thus, he sent letters to King Siva in Seru-nagara and to King Mahānāga in Loṇa-nagara, saying:
"Tomorrow, having adorned your elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and so forth with golden ornaments..."
"Let us all, together with our own people, put on festive attire and assemble while making offerings to the noble Elder Tissa.
When those kings heard this message, they each adorned their elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry according to their respective wealth;
they applied scented unguents to their five fingers, had themselves adorned with golden garlands and other ornaments, and did likewise even for their great oxen.

Having adorned themselves and caused golden breastplates to be fastened upon their horns, the ministers, householders, sons of brahmins, elephant-keepers, dwarfs, hunchbacks, generals, and others—having dressed in variegated garments and smeared themselves with various kinds of ointments—arrived and presented themselves to the king.
The king, surrounded by a fourfold army, mounted the back of a decorated elephant. And the other kings...
Surrounded by their respective retinues and seated upon the backs of elephants, they went forth with the king in their midst, paying homage from the left and right sides.
His departure, however, for the purpose of seeing the Tathāgata, was like Ajātasattu’s journey to the Jīvakambavana; it extended for thirty yojanas to the back of the elephant Erāvaṇa.
Having ascended [the chariot] and being surrounded by the gods in the two divine worlds, it was as if it were the time for Sakka,
lord of the devas, to depart for the Nandana Grove. When the shadow had reached the length of one-and-a-half months,
he departed from the city of Soma and stood at the edge of Lake Seruda, having fivefold musical instruments played by various beautifully adorned and prepared dancing girls.
It was as if the great earth were splitting apart, as if the mountains were overturning, and as if the great ocean were breaking over the land.
Brahmins and auspicious chanters of victory uttered words of blessing.
Women adorned with every ornament set the fivefold musical instruments playing. The great multitude raised thousands of shouts of joy.
He caused it to be performed. Then the king, having had many perfumes, lamps, incense, and other offerings brought, rose up and, surrounded by his army, entered the Elder’s dwelling place.
Having paid homage to the Elder, he sat down and said: "Venerable sir, it is time for the kings to assemble and for the water of donation to be offered.
When the Elder heard his words, he accepted, saying: "It is auspicious, Great King."
On that day of offering the water of donation, various kinds of colorful banners and flags were fastened to poles made of diverse and variegated gems, and they were raised aloft.
Pleasant breezes blew from the eastern and other directions. Likewise, the thousand-rayed maker of light, blazing with a great web of radiance, had set.
It was free from the obstructions of spreading rays, royal dust, Rāhu, clouds, and the like.
Devoid of [other] stars and surrounded by a host of constellations, the full moon rose from the eastern quarter like a bright silver mirror-disk.
At that moment, they lit the staff-lamps and other lights. They adorned the Mahāmaṅgala Cetiya by encircling it with a garland-wreath of *jātisumana* flowers, as if it were a single string of pearls.
Just as the full moon is surrounded by a host of stars, so too...

The Great Shrine, adorned with a garland of lamps, shone exceedingly. Furthermore, all the trees throughout the entire island of Laṅkā became variegated with unseasonal fruits and foliage, as if adorned with diverse banners.
Even the salt-oceans and seas of the great deep were covered with the five kinds of lotuses.
All of them, adorned with various garments and ornaments, resembling gods in appearance,
were numerous, joyful, and delighted.
The people surrounded him on all sides.
They all lit up the beautiful staff-lamp,
and at that time, this entire island was illuminated.
Surrounded by a host of stars, he shone like the full moon standing in the midst of the autumnal sky with its beautiful rays;
even so does this excellent stupa, well-adorned and brilliantly radiant.
In the midst of that garland of lamps, the supreme mountain shines.
All the trees of this island of Laṅkā were entirely covered with banners,
as it were, and they yielded flowers and fruits.
Just as all those who were conscious then performed worship,
so too did all those who were unconscious perform no small amount of worship.

Starting from the majority of the earth-dwelling deities up to the Akanittha deities and Brahmā, they offered divine garlands, *pāricchattaka* flowers, *koviḷāra* flowers, sandalwood powder, and so forth.
They were unable to discern whether [the beings] had come from the celestial realms or from the human world.
It was a vast and great assembly. On that day as well, the great earth, the sky, Mount Yugandhara, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the Uttama mountains, and so forth, all trembled.
Seeing this, the king was filled with exceeding joy; he gathered the Elders, the remaining high ministers, and others, as well as the actors and dancers.

Having taken [the requisites], he went to the courtyard of the shrine, thinking, ‘Right now I shall give the donation for the monastery. The Elder, too, having taken the community of monks, sat down in the decorated pavilion in the courtyard of the shrine.
The king, taking a golden pitcher filled with scented perfumed water, poured the water into the Elder’s hand and gave the donation. Having given it, he spoke thus:
"Noble lady, this relic has come down to me through my paternal lineage.
Now, having brought it from our exceedingly beautiful and delightful Rohaṇa province, we have had a relic chamber constructed of gold and a relic pavilion of the seven precious gems built;
therein we have seated a golden image of the Buddha and enshrined the frontal bone relic of our Ten-Powered Lord for the sake of the noble one’s robes and other requisites."

"Now I shall give you sixteen excellent villages," he said. Having thus granted the excellent villages, he had a drum beaten throughout the Serudatta district, which measured thirty *gāvutas* on all sides, and having appointed them as monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), he said: "Venerable sirs, you must go this very day to the sixteen villages given by me to you.
And having gone, you must take possession of them this very day. Having spoken thus, he entered his own residence. Then...
Having come every day for seven days and given a great almsgiving, on the seventh day he provided the great community of bhikkhus with robes sufficient for the three garments and excellent food;
then he approached the Elder and announced, "Venerable Sir, I have completed all that was to be done in the monastery without omission;
I shall now go home. Having heard his words, the Elder accepted it, saying, "Excellent, Great King."
Furthermore, having had a flower garden constructed for the purpose of worshipping the Cetiya, he provided a livelihood for the garland-makers.
Likewise, having demarcated land at the boundary of the monastery with a golden plough for the drummers and actors, he also established a village for the monastery attendants (*ārāmikas*).
For the sake of service to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he [provided] five hundred daughters of his own ministers who were in his presence...
Having given away so many sons of ministers as well as male and female slaves, he caused five hundred thousand *kahāpaṇas* to be granted to each of them for the purpose of their travel expenses.
Furthermore, he caused sixteen thousand *kahāpaṇas* to be granted to the Saṅgha of monks for the purpose of worshipping the relics.
Then, having summoned Giri-Abhaya, he said: "Dear son, you must dwell here permanently. And in our monastery..."
Having exhorted him, saying, "Be diligent toward the monastery attendants and the noble ones," he entrusted everything to him. The Elder said to him:

"Great King, a great boundary must be established all around. When [the king] said, "Bind it, venerable sir," [the Elder replied], "Great King, it is not possible to bind a boundary by means of an unproclaimed sign;
rather, from the east, west, north, and south of the monastery—"
"Identify the markers for binding the great boundary and give them to us; we shall bind the boundary," he said.
The king, being pleased, adorned seven ministers with all kinds of ornaments, had them designate the boundary markers, and dispatched them to return [with the information].
Those seven ministers, having identified the markers in the four directions, wrote them down on a leaf and brought it back.

They gave it to the king. Having given one hundred kahāpaṇas to each person and having ordered protection to be provided in the four directions, the king informed the great Saṅgha of monks, saying, "Let them bind the boundary.
Then the Elder, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, sat down in the courtyard of the Cetiya;
on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vappa, he bound the boundary and completed the work.
In this regard, the boundary markers (*sīmānimitta*) should be understood as follows: In the eastern direction, there is a jackal-stone (*sigālapāsāṇa*).
From there, passing along the left side of the village of Macchasela, it leaves behind the village-field named Koṭasīmā and reaches Gaṇadvāragāma.
From the northern end of the Cittavāpi reservoir, it passes through the Varagāma field and reaches the back-stone (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*). From there, it goes to the *madhuka* tree named Sālika.
He went to the Ṭhītapāsāṇa Stūpa. From there he went to the Kaṇikāra Rock at the southern corner of the Vāpiyā named Vuttika.
From there he went to the Channajjhāpita Rock. From there he went to the stūpa situated on the Madhuka tree belonging to the lay follower named Kukkuṭasiva.
From there he went to the rock named Soṇḍa. From there he went to the rock named Sabara.
From there he went to Elālatittha. From there, having gone by way of the middle ford through the ravine, he reached the place called Assabandhana.
From there he went to the banyan tree named Udakakāka on the top of a rock;
that tree received its name from the fact that water-crows had lived there. From there he went to Tambatittha, [the site] of the Mahācārikassana Stūpa road.
He went there. Then he went to the back of the hermitage circle. Then he went to the stone stupa standing by the side of the great kadamba tree.
Then he went to the great banyan tree standing at the northern end of the Great Rājuvāpī pond. Then he went to the back of the great forest.
Then he went to the silver mountain at the edge of the salt ocean. Turning back again, he went to the very same Sigāla rock.
Having demarcated this much area on all sides, the king gave it [to him].
After causing many monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and various requisites to be provided for the monastery, and having caused all the walls, gate-towers, and so forth to be constructed,
he completed the monastery and returned to Rohaṇa.
The king, with a heart full of faith, possessed of great merit and great power,
having caused to be built a most excellent stupa resplendent with gold and silver,
and having then caused the boundary and the sixteen villages of Vaṭṭagāma to be demarcated.
Having given all the requisites to the monastery attendants,
he then went to Rohaṇa preceded by a great army;
there he dwelt together with Queen Vihāradevī, rejoicing.
But the Elder, remaining right there, declared: "Whoever dwells in this monastery shall be as if they had lived in the Tathāgata’s own Perfumed Chamber.

From that time forth, surrounded by those whose taints were destroyed—who had attained virtue, conduct, concentration, meditative attainments, the supernormal powers, and the analytical knowledges—he dwelt for a long time recollecting all the qualities of a Buddha, and right there, in the state of Nibbāna without residue...
He attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna.
The Elder Tissa, endowed with manifold virtues and possessed of great learning,
having brought people together in harmony, was extinguished, free from all taints.
Those elders too, endowed with virtue and concentration,
learned, delighting in noble qualities,
and possessing minds arisen through the power of wisdom—
Tens of millions of people, mines of virtue,
have abandoned the cycle of existence; having broken through the analytical knowledges,
these gentle ones have severed their bonds and brought name-and-form to an end.
Having established the supreme peace for beings and gathered the people together,
those of great wisdom, well-minded, have attained nibbāna like lamps.
Thus ends the *Dhātuvamso*, composed for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the noble ones.

By means of this, the monasteries caused to be built should be mentioned: the Vihāradevī Mahāvihāra, the Chātapabbata Vihāra, and the Samudda Vihāra.
The Cittalapabbata Vihāra, the Bhaddapāsāṇadvāra Vihāra, the Acchagalla Vihāra,
the Koḷambatissapabbata Vihāra, the Gaṇa Vihāra, the Kālakā Vihāra, the Dukkha-pālaka Vihāra, the Uccaṅgaṇa Vihāra, and the Koṭitissa Vihāra—
having given these a single name and having had them constructed, including the Tissamahāvihāra at Mahāgāma, one hundred and twenty-eight monasteries were established.
The illustrious king, together with Queen Vihāradevī, caused one hundred and twenty-eight magnificent monasteries to be built.
From that time forth, the king gave great alms and performed meritorious deeds; when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods.
Having performed manifold meritorious deeds, O one of great renown,
and having accomplished the welfare of people, he went to the Tusita city.
There, rejoicing, he enjoyed celestial splendor for a long time.
Endowed with great majesty and honored by the deities,
he will come, desiring that even such worldly success— though it be delightful to the living beings in this world— is for the sake of delusion;
instead, he seeks the supramundane, auspicious, and secure state.
Passing away from there, he will be reborn in Jambudīpa as Subrahmā, the father of the Blessed One Metteyya.
His mother will be the Brahmin woman Brahmavatī, the consort of the monastery.
Prince Abhayagāmaṇī will be the first noble disciple of that Blessed One Metteyya; his younger brother, Saddhātissa, will be the second noble disciple.
With this much, the commentary on the forehead relic is completed.
The lineage of relics is finished.
By means of this meritorious deed, while wandering through various states of existence;
May I be wise in every respect, possessed of wisdom like Sāriputta himself.
Having gone forth in the teaching of the Buddha,
the Vanquisher of Māra, and having attained Nibbāna, may I be released from the bonds of existence.
By this, may I, in all states of existence,
be solely compassionate toward others; may I be of noble birth,
strong, and possessed of mindfulness and wisdom.
May he who is always endowed with the lineage of poets become the foremost among those possessed of wisdom.
